# Why a capability layer

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/about/mission/why-a-capability-layer

An agent can see a button without knowing what business operation it performs, whether the current user may perform it, or what changed afterwards. The common failure in real systems is not that the model cannot click. It is that the page never states, in a machine-readable form, what it permits an agent to do.

A capability layer supplies that missing information.

## A real business operation

Consider an order administration page with a filter panel on the left, an order table in the middle, and an edit dialog on the right. A user asks:

> Change the delivery note on SO-1002 to "deliver by Friday", then save it.

For a person, the task is clear: find SO-1002, open the editor, fill in the note, save, and check that the row reflects the change.

For an agent, the page starts as a set of DOM nodes. From `button`, `input`, and `div` elements alone, it cannot establish:

- which row is SO-1002, or whether the target moves when the list changes;
- which field is the delivery note and which is an internal comment;
- whether Save commits the order or only closes the dialog;
- whether the current user may edit this order, or whether approval is required;
- whether a failed save means validation, permission, network, or stale business state;
- whether a successful response actually changed the order.

If the agent infers from a screenshot and the DOM, it is guessing intent. If it calls an internal API directly, it may bypass validation and approval implemented by the page. If every application writes a private automation script, each integration becomes a one-off project.

## The DOM describes an interface, not a business capability

Consider this button:

```html
<button class="btn btn-danger">Delete</button>
```

The markup does not say which record will be deleted, whether deletion can be undone, whether confirmation is required, whether the current user is allowed to perform it, or what should be observed afterwards. People fill those gaps with domain knowledge, layout, and context. An agent does not have the same reliable priors.

The question is therefore not:

> "How do we make an agent better at clicking buttons?"

It is:

> **"How does a page state which business operations exist, when an agent may execute them, and how the result can be verified?"**

That is what a capability layer answers.

## What a capability layer contains

A capability layer is neither a backend API document nor a chat window. It contains at least four kinds of information.

### Declaration

The page declares the available actions beside its business code: name and meaning, inputs, target record, risk level, and confirmation requirement. A declaration belongs to the application, not to a model prompt. The model may read it; it may not invent it.

### Context

The agent needs facts about the current page: route, visible regions, record window, selection, available actions, reasons an action is unavailable, and which fields must be masked or referenced indirectly. Context should be a bounded business view, not the entire DOM or frontend store.

### Control

"The page declares this action" and "this execution is allowed" are different statements. Control also involves user identity, agent identity, application and tenant, session scope, consent, human approval, and amount or rate limits. The page cannot replace final authorization by the business backend.

### Result

After execution, the agent needs to know whether the action was accepted, which record it affected, what the page observed, and where it failed. Without a result that can be checked, "done" is only a sentence.

## How it relates to other approaches

### Direct backend access

Backend APIs are appropriate for stable service-to-service integration, but they are not a complete expression of page capabilities. An agent must understand internal APIs and may bypass page-level validation, approval, and business constraints. The backend should remain the final authority for authorization and execution; the capability layer gives it an accurate description of the action the user intended.

### Browser automation and vision

CDP, Playwright, and visual agents address how to operate a pixel interface. They are useful for third-party sites that cannot integrate. Inside a controlled application, they still suffer from unstable targeting and results that are difficult to explain. A capability layer does not reject automation; it provides a more precise path where the page can declare one.

### A private in-page assistant

A chat window backed by private APIs can ship quickly, but its capabilities remain locked inside one client. If the same actions must also be available to a user's own agent or a third-party client, the capability model must be separated from that client implementation.

## What changes after adoption

| Role | DOM or private APIs only | An explicit capability layer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frontend developer | Every agent integration explains the page again | Declare once beside business code; reuse across clients |
| Application team | Hard to state what an agent may do | An explicit capability scope, risk levels, and failure boundary |
| Agent | Infers from DOM, screenshots, and labels | Reads business declarations and submits arguments |
| User | Sees only the final reply | Sees the target, confirmation, result, and failure reason |
| Security and audit | Inspects API logs only | Correlates session, action, record, and approval |

## The execution loop

```text
Business page
  │ declares actions, records, regions, and read-only state
  ▼
Capability layer
  │ produces bounded agent context
  ▼
Model or agent runtime
  │ selects an action and submits arguments
  ▼
Page executor
  │ availability, confirmation, validation, business handler
  ▼
Result and observable change
```

The important point is not that an agent manipulates the DOM. It operates on business capabilities declared by the page. The DOM is still present; it is no longer the primary source of business meaning.

## What a capability layer does not guarantee

- It does not make an application secure by itself. Backend authorization, tenant isolation, secret management, and database rules are still required.
- It does not prevent an agent with browser-level access from bypassing the contract. It improves the declared path.
- It does not choose the application's risk policy. The business still decides where confirmation, approval, or dual review is required.
- It does not eliminate model errors. It makes those errors easier to bound, observe, and correct.

## When it is worth adopting

A capability layer is usually appropriate when:

- operations have clear business meaning and change real state;
- the same operations must serve an in-page assistant, an external agent, or several clients;
- the team must explain who initiated an operation, which record it affected, and whether it was approved;
- DOM automation is too brittle, while direct backend access would bypass the interface.

For a one-off demonstration, an uncontrollable third-party page, or operations without stable business semantics, browser automation or a human workflow may be the better choice.

## Common misconceptions

**"A capability layer is just another backend API."** No. It describes business actions performed through the interface. A backend API is one implementation.

**"If an action is declared, it can always execute."** No. Availability, session scope, user confirmation, and backend authorization still apply.

**"A capability layer replaces Playwright."** No. Pages that cannot integrate may still require browser automation.

**"A confirmation dialog makes the operation safe."** Not by itself. Confirmation expresses present intent; it does not replace backend checks for authority and high-risk business rules.

## Continue reading

[What Pling is, and is not](/about/mission/what-pling-is-and-is-not) separates the SDK, page runtime, agent, Surface, and specification, and explains which part owns each responsibility.

# What Pling is, and is not

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/about/mission/what-pling-is-and-is-not

Suppose an order page has two buttons side by side: **Approve** and **Reject**. A person can see the difference immediately. A DOM tree reports two buttons. A screenshot shows where they are. Neither tells an agent, on its own, which business operation each button performs, whether the current user may perform it, whether confirmation is required, or which order will change.

That gap is where Pling operates.

## In one sentence

**Pling is the agent capability layer for web applications.** A page declares its executable operations once, beside the business code. Pling exposes those actions, their targets, bounded context, and execution results to an in-page assistant or, through Agent Surface, to an external agent.

The page remains the application. It owns state, validation, business rules, and access decisions. Pling defines how an application describes the actions it chooses to expose and how an execution is reported.

Models, agent runtimes, and browser automation tools are outside this layer. Pling does not decide what an agent should attempt next.

## The responsibilities behind one operation

These responsibilities are often described together as "the agent". Separating them makes their limits much clearer.

| Responsibility | What it decides | Typical implementation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Host application | What is true, valid, and permitted in this business system | The Vue, React, Vanilla, or jQuery application and its backend |
| Pling SDK and page runtime | Which actions exist, which record they affect, whether they are available, and what happened after execution | `@plingjs/core`, `@plingjs/dom`, and the framework adapters |
| In-page assistant (optional) | What to do next and how to reply to the user | `@plingjs/agent` and the assistant interface chosen by the application |
| Agent Surface | What an external agent may discover and invoke | The page-side Surface implementation |
| Surface specification | Which rules independent implementations must share | `pling.surface/0.1`, currently a public draft |
| External agent runtime | Which agent, model, or client is operating the page | The user's agent, another application, or an extension |

These roles may be delivered together, but they are not interchangeable. The in-page assistant is only one client. The declarations define Pling.

## What the page exposes

For each declared action, Pling gives the agent the information needed to decide: business meaning, target, current availability, confirmation requirement, and the result of an execution.

The page may also expose related records, read-only state, validation messages, and feedback. This view is intentionally narrow. The agent does not receive the whole DOM, the whole frontend store, or every backend field. A smaller, structured view is easier to reason about and keeps unrelated or sensitive data out of the model context.

Sensitive values can be masked or referenced while the page keeps the real value for display and execution. A model may refer to a customer without learning the customer's full identity document number.

## A declaration is not a second business implementation

When an agent invokes an action, the page runs the same handler, validation, and state transition that a user would trigger. The declaration describes the entry point and its constraints; it does not duplicate the business logic.

The result must be more specific than "done". It should identify the action, the target, whether execution succeeded, what the page observed afterwards, and whether a confirmation or human handoff took place. That is what allows an assistant or audit system to distinguish a completed action from an attempted one.

## Actions that are not declared

An action that is not declared is outside the page's capability surface. An in-page assistant must not invent a fallback by finding a similar button with a selector or guessing from a screenshot.

```text
No declaration
    → not part of the capability surface
    → cannot be invoked by the in-page assistant
    → no selector or screenshot fallback
```

This rule has a clear limit. An external agent with browser-level access, such as one using the Chrome DevTools Protocol, can still interact with the page outside Pling's contract. That is a different permission boundary. Pling does not claim to prevent every form of browser automation.

In all cases, the backend remains responsible for final authorization. A page can establish that `approve_order` exists. It cannot establish, by itself, that a particular user may approve a particular amount at this particular time.

## One declaration, two clients

An application can offer an assistant inside its own interface. It can also expose the same declarations to a user's external agent through Agent Surface. These are two ways to use one page model, not two separate integrations.

The in-page assistant suits an application that wants to provide a complete experience without requiring another installation. An external agent suits a user who already has an agent and wants it to work under the application's terms. Changing clients should not require redeclaring the page.

## What it does not replace

Pling is not a model, a reasoning engine, or a prompt-management system. It is not a replacement for Vue, React, or another frontend framework, and it is not a selector-based browser automation tool.

It does not replace backend authorization, rate limits, tenant isolation, secret management, workflow systems, or human review. Those systems answer different questions. Pling makes the page-side contract explicit; it does not compress every security decision into the page.

For a third-party page that cannot integrate, browser automation or visual interaction may remain the practical option. Pling addresses the case where the page owner can declare what the page does and under which conditions an agent may act.

## What you can rely on today

The current SDK supports declarations, target resolution, execution, and result reporting. The reference implementation includes both an in-page assistant and an external Surface client.

`pling.surface/0.1` is still a public draft. It is published so implementations can be compared and reviewed, and it may change. Pling is not yet a cross-vendor standard, and this documentation does not describe it as one.

The narrower claim is supported today: an integrated page can expose a bounded set of business actions to an agent, execute them through the page, and return a result. Production suitability still depends on the application's own authorization, data, and operational boundaries.

## Continue reading

To understand how declarations relate to consent, delegation, and audit, continue with [Trust, authority, and audit](/about/mission/trust-authority-and-audit).

To integrate an application, start with the [Vue quick start](/vue/quick-start-add-pling-to-a-vue-app) or [React quick start](/react/quick-start-add-pling-to-a-react-app). The concepts are shared; the integration paths differ.

# Trust, authority, and audit

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/about/mission/trust-authority-and-audit

Alice works in an order operations team. She asks an external agent to approve order SO-1002 for ¥48,000. The order page contains an **Approve** button, and Alice is signed in.

Those facts still do not establish that this approval should happen. The system also needs to know which user is represented, which agent is acting, which application session the request belongs to, what that session may use, whether this amount requires another approver, and what record remains afterwards.

An agent can find a button without acquiring the authority to use it. Trust begins when those questions have explicit answers.

## The parties behind an external operation

An external write involves at least four parties. Combining them into a single "signed-in user" obscures who is responsible for what.

| Party | Question | Evidence the host may rely on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User | Whose business identity and authority are being used? | SSO or application session |
| Agent | Which program is acting? | Agent identifier, client identity, or delegation record |
| Application session | Where and for how long may this agent act? | Origin, tenant, session id, scope, expiry |
| Business backend | Is this operation allowed on this resource now? | Role, ownership, limits, approval, transaction rules |

A delegation is not a fifth identity. It records a relationship: user U allowed agent G to use capability set C in application A until time T. The user still owns the authority; the agent is still the actor. Audit must retain both.

## Declaration, exposure, and authority

Three distinct statements are often compressed into "the agent can approve orders":

1. **The page declares the action.** `approve_order` exists and has a business description, inputs, target, and effect.
2. **This session exposes the action.** The site's exposure policy and the session's scope both allow it.
3. **The backend permits this specific execution.** The signed-in user may approve this order, for this amount, at this time.

The first statement describes software structure. The second describes the boundary of one agent session. The third is a business decision.

Pling can establish the first two and hand the result to the page executor. It cannot replace the third. A page declaration is not a permission grant, and a session scope does not overrule the backend.

In the current Surface implementation, the host supplies an already verified session. The callable set is the intersection of the site-level exposure policy and that session's scope. Expiry and revocation are checked at the session boundary; rate limits and replay protection are separate guards. None of these checks turns the page into the final authorization authority.

## Consent, confirmation, and approval

These mechanisms answer different questions and have different lifetimes.

| Mechanism | Question | Typical lifetime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delegation consent | May this agent use this set of capabilities for this period? | A session or a longer bounded grant |
| Operation confirmation | Does the user want to execute this action now? | One action, or a deliberately chosen short-lived allowance |
| Backend approval | Has an authorized approver approved this exact high-risk operation in a form the backend can verify? | One business operation |

A confirmation dialog can express intent. It is not, by itself, a backend-verifiable approval. If the operation needs a second approver, an amount limit, or an auditable receipt, that decision belongs to the business backend. The page may collect the response through a trusted host flow; an agent's claim that approval happened is not evidence.

The reverse is also true. A valid long-lived delegation does not mean every exposed action may run without confirmation. A high-risk action may require a fresh human decision even while the delegation is valid.

The `confirm` field in an action declaration is combined with the risk level to produce a confirmation policy. When `confirm` is omitted, risk level decides by default: a dangerous action asks for confirmation instead of being silently allowed by a configuration gap. The application still decides whether page confirmation is sufficient or a backend approval is required.

## Approval material must not enter agent context

When a backend approves a specific operation, the approval should be bound to facts that cannot be silently swapped:

- the user and agent;
- the application session;
- the capability and target record;
- a canonical hash of the execution arguments;
- the request id and an expiry time.

The receipt token or verification secret stays between the trusted page flow and the approval backend. It must not be returned to the agent, placed in model context, written to ordinary logs, or reused for another request.

The Surface protocol can carry a public approval association id for audit purposes. The executor reports that id; the protocol records it in the audit event and removes it from the agent-visible response. This preserves the link between approval and execution without turning the agent into a courier for approval material.

## What an audit event must answer

Audit should make the authorization and execution chain reconstructable without copying the business payload. A practical minimum is:

| Field group | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| User, agent, session, delegation | Establish who acted under which relationship |
| Request id, capability, record | Identify the attempted operation |
| Outcome, error code, duration | Distinguish success, business rejection, denial, and failure |
| Approval association id | Link a high-risk execution to the enterprise's approval record |

Raw arguments, response bodies, cookies, JWTs, and approval tokens do not belong in the default audit stream. They may contain personal data or secrets, and retention requirements differ by jurisdiction and business domain. If an application needs argument-level evidence, its backend should define, encrypt, and restrict that record.

The current Surface implementation exposes an audit sink that receives metadata only. `@plingjs/server` follows the same principle for model requests: it records request metadata and outcomes without storing prompts or response bodies by default. Persistence, retention, and access remain host responsibilities.

## Failure must refuse, not widen access

Trust is tested when information is missing or inconsistent. The safe response is to refuse execution, not to infer a nearby permission.

| Condition | Required behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| No verified session | Reject the request |
| Expired or revoked session | Reject immediately and require a new grant |
| Capability outside the exposed scope | Reject without widening the allowlist |
| Target record disappeared | Report the missing target; do not choose a similar record |
| User declines confirmation | Stop; do not retry with a different prompt |
| Backend rejects the operation | Preserve the business error and its actionable context |
| Audit delivery fails | Keep the business result unchanged, but raise an operational alert |

This is fail-closed behaviour: unknown, expired, unverifiable, or conflicting facts produce a refusal. A successful response means every required check passed.

## Five questions to answer before deployment

1. Which actions change business state, and which only read data?
2. How is each target record identified stably?
3. Which actions require confirmation, and which also require backend approval or human handoff?
4. Which user, agent, tenant, and capability scope does the session bind, and when does it expire?
5. Which audit metadata must be retained, and which raw data must be excluded?

Answer these first in a low-risk workflow, then extend the same rules to refunds, approvals, publishing, and other irreversible operations. A simple workflow should not be slowed by an enterprise approval stack. A high-risk workflow should not be made to look solved by a popup.

## Limits of the current implementation

The current Surface implementation accepts only an already verified session, intersects site exposure with session scope, rejects expired or revoked sessions, supports request rate limits and replay protection, emits metadata-only audit events, and removes approval material from the agent-visible response.

`@plingjs/delegation` is an optional reference package for short-lived, scoped agent credentials. It supports issuing, introspecting, rotating, and revoking credentials. A token is returned only when issued or refreshed, and the reference store keeps only a hash. Identity providers, durable storage, event delivery, SSO, tenant policy, and audit retention remain application responsibilities.

Pling does not define an enterprise RBAC or ABAC model, provide a production approval service, store audit records for you, or certify a deployment. It provides a shared page boundary: which capabilities were exposed, which execution occurred, and which checkable information accompanied the result.

## Continue reading

If a page must exchange capabilities with independent clients, [From a single-site integration to an open protocol](/about/mission/from-single-site-bridge-to-open-protocol) explains when a private bridge needs to become a protocol.

For the deployment threat list and operational checks, read the [Security and trust center](/security/). For the boundary between page capabilities and external clients, read [What is Agent Surface](/surface/).

# From single-site bridge to open protocol

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/about/mission/from-single-site-bridge-to-open-protocol

When one page serves one in-page assistant, a private bridge is often enough. The page registers an action for the assistant, the assistant invokes it by agreement, and the team can iterate quickly without defining a public standard.

The problem changes when another client must operate the same page. The new client has to relearn the page's actions, and the next page has to adapt to the existing client again. What is missing is not another RPC layer, but shared meaning for four things: what a capability is, what the caller may observe, who may invoke it, and what the result proves.

That is where a protocol earns its place. It exists not because a system is distributed, but because independent implementations must agree on the same facts.

## Where a private bridge stops working

Consider an order page already connected to an in-page assistant. The assistant calls `approve_order` through a private object and reads component state directly. This can work well inside one product, but it ties four concerns together:

- how the page describes an action;
- how the assistant discovers it;
- how both sides represent session and authority;
- how execution results return to the assistant.

When a second client appears, those agreements are either copied or replaced by a near-equivalent. After copying, the page maintains two semantics. After replacement, the same action may imply a different target, confirmation rule, or error behaviour in each client.

Browser automation addresses a different problem. CDP, Playwright, and visual agents can operate an interface without a page contract, which is appropriate when the page cannot or will not declare capabilities. They cannot reliably answer whether a button reads or irreversibly changes state, whether a second approver is required, which records an agent may reference, or whether a failed call already changed business state.

When several implementations must answer those questions in the same way, a protocol becomes necessary.

## What the protocol has to define

`pling.surface/0.1` reduces the problem to four kinds of object:

1. **Capability.** A business operation the page chooses to expose, including its inputs, effect, and confirmation requirement.
2. **Context.** A bounded, read-only view needed for the current decision.
3. **Session.** Which user an agent represents, in which application boundary, until when, and with which capability scope.
4. **Result.** Whether the request was understood, whether execution occurred, whether business state changed, and what can be observed next.

Transport, authentication, business authorization, storage, and model execution are outside the protocol. The contract can run over `postMessage`, MCP, HTTP, or another transport without changing the business meaning of a capability.

## Design goals

The protocol is deliberately small. These goals constrain both the data model and observable behaviour.

| Goal | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Discovery without the DOM | A caller obtains page identity and available capabilities from a structured response |
| Business semantics | Actions are named by business intent, not selectors or visual position |
| Bounded observation | Context is selective and bounded; it is not the whole DOM or application store |
| Explicit control | Session scope, expiry, revocation, confirmation, and backend authorization are represented separately |
| Actionable results | Responses distinguish protocol errors, execution errors, and business effects |
| Transport independence | The same contract can run over more than one transport |
| Fail closed | Unknown versions, unknown methods, out-of-scope capabilities, and unavailable guards are rejected |

The protocol provides no general browser API. It has no `click(selector)`, `eval(script)`, or equivalent escape hatch. It does not authenticate users, make business authorization decisions, store credentials, or replace MCP. These exclusions define the boundary; they are not temporary omissions.

## Core model

Let `C_page` be the capabilities declared by the page and `C_session` the capabilities allowed by a verified session. The effective set is:

```text
C_eff = C_page ∩ C_session
```

Both `describe` and `invoke` operate on `C_eff`. A capability outside that set cannot be discovered or invoked through the session, even if the page declared it globally.

Three decisions must remain distinct:

| Decision | Question | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declaration | Does the page implement this capability? | Page application |
| Exposure | Is the capability inside this session's scope? | Host and session validation |
| Authorization | May this user perform this operation on this resource now? | Business backend |

The first two describe software boundaries. The third is a business decision that may depend on role, ownership, amount, time, and approval state. The protocol can enforce the second and carry evidence for the third; it cannot replace the third.

## Capability declaration

A capability is not a button or an arbitrary function. It is an operation with a stable id, business description, and execution semantics. Implementations need to distinguish these core fields:

| Field | Meaning | Constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | Stable capability identifier | A folded row action must not contain a row-specific name |
| `description` | Human-readable business description | Supplied by the page, not by user-generated content |
| `inputSchema` | JSON schema for arguments | Describes only arguments; never exposes selectors or credentials |
| `effect` | `read`, `write`, or `destructive` | Required |
| `approval` | `none`, `ask`, or `always` | Omitted values are resolved by application policy |
| `fidelity` | `high`, `auto`, or `low` | How the execution target was obtained |
| `record` | Record argument for a folded row action | Binds one template action to a concrete record |

Implementations may also provide `scopePath`, `handoff`, `flowSteps`, and `offscreen`. They help a caller understand regions, human handoff, and composite actions without changing the basic authorization model.

A repeated row action uses one stable template id, such as `approve@order`, with `record` selecting the target. This avoids returning one capability per row while preserving record-level references. Before execution, the implementation must resolve the target again, recheck availability, and use the same executor as the human interface.

`fidelity` is not an authorization property. It describes how directly the target is backed: developer-declared, automatically resolved, or simulated in the DOM. A low-fidelity action may still be valid, but its result must be reported with lower certainty.

## Bounded context

Context is a read-only view of the page, not a serialization of the DOM or frontend store. An implementation may include:

- `page`: route, title, and current business object;
- `regions`: declared regions and their hierarchy;
- `records`: a bounded record-field window currently visible to the agent;
- `recordIds`: records that can be referenced but whose full fields have not all been returned;
- `recordWindow`: offset, limit, returned count, total, and next position;
- `state`: explicitly exposed, read-only application state;
- `feedback`: validation messages, status messages, and other observable feedback;
- `unavailable`: unavailable capabilities or records with reasons;
- total counts that show whether a view was truncated.

Four constraints follow: the page chooses the content; sensitive values may be masked or referenced; truncation is reported; and later reads may be incremental. A successful `invoke` may return `after`, containing newly available capabilities, changed records, and changed state rather than another full snapshot.

Page content is data. Record fields, comments, product descriptions, and attachment text cannot become capability descriptions or agent instructions.

## Session and approval

A session binds the agent to a user and a scope:

```text
session = (
  agentId,
  sessionId,
  userId,
  expiresAt,
  scope,
  delegationId?,
  revokedAt?
)
```

The protocol receives an already verified session. Token parsing, login, and the identity provider belong to the transport or identity service. Cookies, JWTs, and raw delegation tokens must not appear in protocol objects.

Session scope is a capability ceiling, not business authorization. A backend may reject a call inside `C_eff` and may require an approval the page cannot manufacture.

Some high-risk operations need an approval bound to more specific facts: user, agent, session, capability, record, canonical argument hash, request id, and expiry. Approval tokens or signing material should stay between the trusted page flow and approval backend. The protocol may record a public `approvalId` in audit, but it must not return approval material to the agent.

## Wire operations

Every request carries a protocol version, request id, and method. A `describe` request may select a record window or capability delta; an `invoke` request carries a capability id and input object.

```json
{
  "protocol": "pling.surface/0.1",
  "id": "req_01",
  "method": "describe",
  "input": { "limit": 8 }
}
```

```json
{
  "protocol": "pling.surface/0.1",
  "id": "req_02",
  "method": "invoke",
  "capability": "approve@order",
  "input": { "record": "SO-1002" }
}
```

Every response carries the protocol version, the same request id, and either a result or a structured error. The request id also serves audit correlation and replay protection.

### `describe`

`describe` is read-only. It returns page identity, the current capability set, bounded context, and session limits. A caller may request specific records, a record window, or a capability delta. The capability list is not a DOM snapshot; it is the set of business actions the page has chosen to expose.

### `invoke`

`invoke` selects a capability from `C_eff`, validates arguments against its schema, and passes the action to the page executor. A successful response contains the execution result and, when the page can observe a change, a bounded `after` delta.

### Errors

Protocol errors and business execution errors are separate. `INVALID_REQUEST`, `PROTOCOL_VERSION_UNSUPPORTED`, `METHOD_NOT_SUPPORTED`, `CAPABILITY_NOT_EXPOSED`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `REPLAY_DETECTED`, and the session error family are protocol-level failures. A page action that fails because a record is unavailable, authority is missing, or a business precondition is unmet returns a structured execution error.

The distinction matters. A protocol error means the request cannot be interpreted or is outside the contract. An execution error means the request was understood, but the page or business refused or failed it. Retrying is safe only when the error says so.

## Execution order

An `invoke` request should be evaluated in this order. The order is part of the security model because it determines which failure is reported and whether side effects are possible.

1. Validate the envelope, protocol version, request id, and method.
2. Resolve the verified session; reject missing, expired, or revoked sessions.
3. Compute `C_eff = C_page ∩ C_session`; reject a capability outside it.
4. Apply the session rate limit; fail closed if the limiter is unavailable.
5. Atomically reserve the request id in the replay guard; reject a duplicate, and fail closed if the guard is unavailable.
6. Resolve the capability and validate its input.
7. Execute through the page executor, preserving the same validation, confirmation, and business path as the human interface.
8. Remove approval material from the agent-visible result and write the audit event.
9. Return the execution result and any bounded `after` observation.

`describe` performs the same session and scope checks but does not reserve a replay id because it does not mutate business state. Rate limits still apply.

Audit failure must not change the business result, but it must not be silent. The implementation reports it through a separate error handler or metric.

## Security invariants

These properties define the protocol boundary. A conforming implementation must preserve them or explicitly document a deviation.

| Invariant | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| No generic DOM control | No selector-based click, script evaluation, or arbitrary browser step |
| Credential isolation | Cookies, JWTs, OAuth tokens, and delegation secrets do not enter protocol or model context |
| Declaration is not authority | A capability in `C_page` is not automatically authorized |
| Scope is an intersection | Effective scope is `C_page ∩ C_session`; no path may silently widen it |
| Fail closed | Unknown versions, unknown methods, out-of-scope capabilities, and unavailable guards are rejected |
| Approval material is not agent-visible | Approval tokens and signing material do not enter the agent response; only an audit association remains |
| Context is bounded | Context is selective and reports omission; it is not the DOM or entire store |
| Audit is metadata-only by default | Arguments and response bodies are not recorded without a separate written host policy |
| Page content is data | User-generated content cannot become a capability description or instruction channel |
| Browser-level bypass is acknowledged | An agent with CDP or equivalent access can bypass the contract; the protocol improves the declared path without claiming to prevent all automation |

The last invariant matters. The protocol cannot guarantee that an agent with lower-level browser access will use the declared path. It can make that path more precise, auditable, and less dependent on visual inference. It cannot turn an untrusted client into a trusted one.

## Relationship to adjacent layers

| Layer | What it decides | Relationship to this protocol |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CDP | How to control a browser instance | A lower-level execution mechanism, not a business contract |
| Playwright and similar automation | How to locate and operate an element | An execution layer for pages without declared capabilities |
| Vision model | What an interface appears to be | A fallback when semantics are unavailable, not an authorization or audit model |
| MCP | How tools are exposed to an agent runtime | A possible transport and tool-calling convention |
| This protocol | What a page offers, what context is visible, and what a result means | A page capability contract that can run over MCP or another transport |
| Business backend | Whether a specific operation is allowed and committed | The final authority for authorization and transaction state |

These layers are not competitors. A page may expose a capability through this contract and still execute it with ordinary HTTP, a database transaction, or an internal workflow. MCP can carry the contract, but MCP alone does not explain what `approve_order` means or prove that an approval is valid.

## What the current draft establishes

The reference implementation supports a capability projection from the page registry; `describe` and `invoke`; session scope, expiry, and revocation; injectable rate limiting and replay protection; bounded context and incremental `after`; folded row actions; audit metadata; and approval stripping from agent-visible responses. The repository includes tests for scope intersection, invalid records, replay, rate limits, audit shape, and approval stripping.

`pling.surface/0.1` remains a public draft. It has not established a complete stable wire schema, independent page-side and client-side implementations, a cross-implementation conformance suite, or `attach`, `observe`, `handoff`, and `detach` as completed protocol methods. Production identity, distributed rate limiting, durable replay protection, and a general audit service are also outside the protocol.

An implementation can therefore be evaluated on narrower questions:

- Can a page expose a declared action without exposing its DOM?
- Can a client invoke it without site-specific selectors?
- Is the effective scope enforced before execution?
- Does the result distinguish "request accepted", "action executed", and "business state changed"?

These questions are testable. Whether the design achieves broad adoption, interoperability across independent implementations, or better outcomes than existing automation still requires deployment and comparative evaluation.

## When a protocol is warranted

When there is one page, one client, and one team, a private bridge may be simpler. A shared contract starts to pay off when the page must serve a user's own agent, several clients, or independent vendors.

Adoption does not require implementing everything at once. A team can start with read-only actions and one low-risk write path, validate discovery, scope, execution, and result semantics, then add approval, delegation, and more transports.

## Continue reading

For the page-side Surface model and its current boundary, read [What is Agent Surface](/surface/). To add the first declared action to a Vue page, continue with the [Vue quick start](/vue/quick-start-add-pling-to-a-vue-app).
