# Actions with input and verified results

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/react/actions-with-input-and-verified-results

The inspector from the previous chapter made an important fact visible. When the user asked to add a task, the first request contained `composer_text` but not `composer_submit`. Only after the input had text did the second request contain the submit button. The model was being asked to reconstruct a form workflow: find the field, fill it, wait for the button to become enabled, then press it.

That integration is accurate to the page, but it is not the operation the user requested. The user asked for one task to be added. This chapter keeps the visible form unchanged and changes what the agent can call: one business action, `add_task`, replaces the two control-level actions.

## Why a form is not yet a business action

A form is a useful interface for a person. It gives the input a place on the page, keeps the submit button close to it, and lets the browser handle focus and keyboard submission. Those details do not have to become the agent's working model.

When the agent is given only the input and the button, it has to infer all of the following:

- which field belongs to the requested operation;
- whether the field must be filled before the button can run;
- whether the button is currently present and available;
- whether pressing it completed the operation.

That inference has three practical costs. One business operation can consume several tool calls. A layout change can make the declarations stale even when the business operation has not changed. And there is no single place to state the argument rules or the result the page should observe.

Moving the declaration to the form does not remove the form. It gives the agent the same entry point the page already uses: the function that adds a task.

| From the user's side | Before this chapter | After this chapter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “Add a task called Reply to the customer.” | Fill the input, then press submit | Call `add_task` with the task text |
| Input rules | The input length and disabled state | A declared `text` parameter |
| “Can I add another?” | The button becomes disabled | `available` returns the reason |
| “Did it work?” | Infer from the changed list | An explicit `expect` result |

## Declare the operation on the form

The React change is local. The input and submit button remain ordinary React elements, and the form still handles manual submission. The two primitive declarations from the previous chapter are replaced by one declaration on the form:

```tsx{6,8-18,20-44}
const [tasks, setTasks] = useState<Task[]>(() =>
  copy.seedTasks.map((task, index) => ({ id: `t${index + 1}`, ...task })),
);
const [draft, setDraft] = useState("");
const sequence = useRef(copy.seedTasks.length);
const lastAddedId = useRef<string | null>(null);

function addTask(value: string): Task | null {
  const text = value.trim();
  if (!text || tasks.length >= MAX_TASKS) return null;
  const task = { id: `t${++sequence.current}`, text, done: false };
  setTasks((current) => [task, ...current]);
  return task;
}

function submitDraft(): void {
  if (addTask(draft)) setDraft("");
}

const addTaskRef = usePlingTool<HTMLFormElement>({
  id: "add_task",
  desc: copy.addTaskDesc,
  kind: "write",
  params: [{
    name: "text",
    label: copy.addTaskParamLabel,
    minLength: 1,
    maxLength: 80,
    pattern: /\S/,
  }],
  available: () =>
    tasks.length < MAX_TASKS ? true : copy.addTaskFullReason,
  run: (args: Record<string, unknown>) => {
    lastAddedId.current = addTask(String(args.text))?.id ?? null;
  },
  expect: {
    desc: copy.addTaskExpect,
    check: () =>
      lastAddedId.current !== null &&
      Boolean(document.querySelector(
        `[data-task-id="${lastAddedId.current}"]`,
      )),
  },
});
```

The form keeps its existing fields. Only the ref moves from the input and button to the form:

```tsx{3,5-8}
<form
  className="composer"
  ref={addTaskRef}
  onSubmit={(event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    submitDraft();
  }}
>
  <label className="composer__label" htmlFor="new-task">{copy.newTaskLabel}</label>
  <div className="composer__row">
    <input
      id="new-task"
      value={draft}
      onChange={(event) => setDraft(event.target.value)}
      autoComplete="off"
      maxLength={80}
      placeholder={copy.placeholder}
    />
    <button
      type="submit"
      disabled={!draft.trim() || tasks.length >= MAX_TASKS}
    >
      {copy.addTask}
    </button>
  </div>
</form>
```

Remove the previous chapter's `composerRef` and `submitRef`; the input and button no longer need separate Pling declarations.

Because the declaration has a `run` function, invoking `add_task` calls that function with the supplied arguments. The framework does not simulate a click on the form. A person can still type and submit normally; both paths enter the same `addTask` function.

`lastAddedId` is a ref because `run` writes it and `expect` reads it later; both callbacks need the same mutable slot. The task list itself remains ordinary React state. `usePlingTool` reads the latest `available` and `run` callbacks from the current render, so neither needs a second copy of the list.

## Describe the input before execution

`params` is the contract for the action's arguments:

```ts
params: [{
  name: "text",
  label: "Task text, 1–80 characters; it cannot contain only spaces",
  minLength: 1,
  maxLength: 80,
  pattern: /\S/,
}]
```

Those field rules are projected into a JSON Schema sent with the tool:

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "text": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Task text, 1–80 characters; it cannot contain only spaces",
      "minLength": 1,
      "maxLength": 80,
      "pattern": "\\S"
    }
  },
  "required": ["text"]
}
```

Parameters are required unless the declaration says `optional: true`. Validation runs before the approval decision and before `run`, so a missing `text`, an empty string, or whitespace-only text returns `INVALID_PARAMS` without opening a confirmation prompt or changing the list.

This contract is about the shape and validity of the operation's input. It is not authorization. A valid task text does not prove that this user may add a task, and a parameter rule must not be used in place of a server-side permission check.

## Connect the action to the existing business function

The declaration does not carry a second implementation of adding tasks:

```ts
run: (args: Record<string, unknown>) => {
  lastAddedId.current = addTask(String(args.text))?.id ?? null;
},
```

The manual form calls `addTask(draft)`. The agent path calls `addTask(text)` through `run`. Task id generation and insertion order stay in one place; `available` and the disabled button communicate the same precondition earlier.

`run` may be asynchronous; the framework waits for its promise before checking the result. Its return value is still not evidence that the page reached the desired state. React may not have committed the row yet, or the application may still be waiting for a request. The next sections supply the missing evidence.

## Report page preconditions

The form is still visible when the list is full, but the business operation cannot add another task. `available` makes that state explicit:

```ts
available: () =>
  tasks.length < MAX_TASKS ? true : copy.addTaskFullReason,
```

The string appears under **Unavailable** in the page snapshot. If a stale action id is executed anyway, the same reason is returned with `ACTION_UNAVAILABLE`. The model can therefore distinguish “this page has no add action” from “this action exists, but the list is full”.

`available` is a page and business precondition, not an authorization decision. At execution time, the framework also checks whether the target is disabled, hidden, covered, or outside the visible area. Region filtering is a separate exposure rule: an action outside the active region is omitted from the snapshot the model receives, but that omission is not a permission check for an already known action id. Server-side authorization remains necessary.

## Make success observable

`add_task` declares what the page should contain after the operation:

```ts
expect: {
  desc: "The new task is present in the list",
  check: () =>
    lastAddedId.current !== null &&
    Boolean(document.querySelector(
      `[data-task-id="${lastAddedId.current}"]`,
    )),
}
```

The check looks for the rendered task row, not only for the id returned by `addTask`. In React, updating state and committing the new row are different moments. After `run`, the framework polls the check for up to two seconds by default; `expect.timeout` can change the bound. If the check succeeds, the execution result includes the description above. If it never succeeds, the result is `EXPECTATION_FAILED`: the operation ran, but the page did not show the declared result.

This prevents two opposite mistakes. Treating an unverified render as success can hide a broken update. Treating it as a failed click can invite a duplicate submission. `expect` records page evidence, but it is not a server acknowledgement, an audit record, or proof that the business result is correct beyond the stated condition.

## The result also carries change evidence

Because the list rows are records, the framework can compare the page before and after the action. A successful add looks like this:

```json
{
  "changed": {
    "observed": true,
    "records": {
      "added": ["t4"],
      "removed": [],
      "updated": [],
      "reordered": false,
      "omitted": { "added": 0, "removed": 0, "updated": 0 },
      "total": { "from": 3, "to": 4 }
    },
    "actions": {
      "added": ["toggle@t4"],
      "removed": [],
      "omitted": { "added": 0, "removed": 0 }
    }
  }
}
```

`expect` answers “did the declared page condition become true?” `changed` answers the narrower question “which exposed records and actions differ between the two snapshots?” Neither replaces the other, and neither is a complete proof of business correctness. A change can match the recorded fields while still being the wrong business outcome.

## Compare the declarations in Activity

The inspector from the previous chapter remains enabled, so this change can be checked without guessing. Send a request to add one task, open **Activity**, and select **Diagnostics**.

In the model call for that request:

1. `Tools sent` contains `add_task`, with a `text` parameter and its validation rules.
2. It does not contain `composer_text` or `composer_submit`; those declarations no longer exist on the page.
3. The response contains one `add_task` call with the supplied text.
4. The next request's **Request messages** contain the tool result, including the expectation description and the record change above.

The number of model calls is not fixed. A model may answer in one step, call the action after reading the page, or stop to ask for a missing detail. What is fixed is the shape of the operation: the agent has one business action to choose, not a form sequence to reconstruct.

## Read failure results correctly

| Result | Meaning | What already happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `INVALID_PARAMS` | The argument is missing or violates the declared rules | Neither confirmation nor the business function ran |
| `ACTION_UNAVAILABLE` | A page or business precondition is not met | The business function did not run; the result includes the reason |
| `EXPECTATION_FAILED` | The function ran, but the declared page result was not observed | The page may have changed; retrying without checking can duplicate the operation |

This is why the declaration separates input validation, availability, execution, and observation. Collapsing them into one boolean makes it impossible to explain which part failed.

## Run and verify

From the repository root:

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev r-05
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5245/`. The runnable example is in `examples/tutorials/r-05-actions-with-input-and-verified-results`; the Chinese interface uses `pnpm tutorial:dev r-05 --locale zh` and `http://127.0.0.1:5245/?lang=zh`.

Check the following:

1. Type `Reply to the customer` into the form and submit it. The task should appear at the top and the input should clear.
2. Ask the assistant: `Add “Prepare tomorrow’s agenda” to my tasks.` The result should use `add_task`, not the form controls.
3. Open **Activity**, then **Diagnostics**. In the request that performed the add, `Tools sent` should contain `add_task` and no `composer_*` action.
4. Expand **Tools sent** and confirm that `add_task` has a `text` parameter with the declared length and whitespace rules.
5. Open the next request and check its tool message for the expectation description and the new record. The list should contain the requested task.
6. Fill the list to eight tasks, then inspect the next request. `add_task` should be absent from **Tools sent** and listed under **Unavailable** with the full-list reason. An unavailable action is filtered out before the model can choose it; calling a stale action id directly would return `ACTION_UNAVAILABLE`.
7. Mark one existing task complete. The row action should still update only that record.

The manual form and the agent path now share one business operation, while the page still works as an ordinary Todo list.

## Next step

The add operation now has a stable identity, validated input, a stated availability rule, and an observable result. The next question is where the declared interaction lands in the DOM. A native input, a component wrapper, and a component with several internal controls can all expose the wrong element unless the target is chosen deliberately.

The next chapter examines real controls and custom components, including when automatic target resolution is trustworthy and when the declaration needs a more precise target.

---

# Real controls and custom components

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/react/real-controls-and-custom-components

The previous chapter replaced the form's two control actions with one business action, `add_task`. That was the right move for adding a task, but it does not follow that every interaction should become a single business operation. A priority selector, a search field, and a filter still belong to the page's ordinary controls. The agent should use those controls; it should not bypass them.

There is a second problem. A declaration can sit on a native element or on a component wrapper. The wrapper rarely receives the event itself. If the framework clicks the wrapper, the page may look unchanged even though the action reported success. This chapter is about that gap: which element actually receives the interaction, and what evidence the framework has for choosing it.

## What the previous chapter leaves open

The added task is still a good starting point. A user may now say:

> Add “Prepare tomorrow's agenda” with later priority, then search for “agenda”.

The add operation already has a business action. The priority and the search are different. They are controls the person can see and use, and their behavior is owned by the page. The agent needs to operate the same controls rather than call an invented `set_priority` or `perform_search` function that does not exist in the application.

Two questions must remain separate:

- **What interaction should happen?** Set a select value, type into a field, press Enter, click one of several buttons, or move the pointer over a menu.
- **Which element receives it?** A native control, a single input inside a component, or one explicitly named button inside a component with several controls.

The first question belongs to the primitive. The second belongs to target resolution. If either one is wrong, a result can say “clicked” while the application did nothing.

## The controls in this example

The page keeps the previous chapter's Todo structure and adds four control patterns:

| Action | Primitive | Intended element | Fidelity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `select_priority` | `select` | the native priority `<select>` | `high` (`native`) |
| `search_text` | `type` | the single input inside `SearchBox` | `auto` |
| `search_enter` | `press` | the same input | `auto` |
| `show_all_tasks` | `click` | one button inside `TaskFilters` | `high` (`declared` target) |
| `show_open_tasks` | `click` | one button inside `TaskFilters` | `high` (`declared` target) |
| `show_completed_tasks` | `click` | one button inside `TaskFilters` | `high` (`declared` target) |
| `open_bulk_menu` | `hover` | the root of `BulkMenu` | `high` (explicit claim) |
| `clear_completed` | `click` | the button mounted inside the open menu | `high` (`native`) |

These are not competing ways to express the same operation. `add_task` is a business operation with its own validation and result condition. The controls above are page interactions. They stay at that level because that is what the page exposes and because the user can see and manipulate them directly.

## A native control needs no target search

The priority selector is a normal React `<select>`. Its value is already controlled by the application:

```tsx{1-11}
const priorityRef = usePlingTool<HTMLSelectElement>({
  id: "select_priority",
  desc: copy.selectPriorityDesc,
  kind: "write",
  action: "select",
  params: [{
    name: "value",
    label: copy.selectPriorityParamLabel,
    values: ["today", "soon", "later"],
  }],
});
```

The declaration does not add a second priority state. The `select` primitive writes the native value and dispatches a `change` event. React's existing `onChange` receives that event and updates the state used by `addTask`.

```tsx{3-6}
<select
  id="task-priority"
  ref={priorityRef}
  value={priority}
  aria-label={copy.priorityAria}
  onChange={(event) => setPriority(event.target.value as Priority)}
>
  <option value="today">{copy.priorities.today}</option>
  <option value="soon">{copy.priorities.soon}</option>
  <option value="later">{copy.priorities.later}</option>
</select>
```

The native element is the target. No descendant search is needed, so the resolved fidelity is `high` with the reason `native`. The `params` declaration is still useful: it says that `value` is required and limits the model to the three values the page can consume.

Changing the priority does not itself create a task. That is why `add_task` still reads the current priority when it runs:

```tsx{2}
run: (args: Record<string, unknown>) => {
  lastAddedId.current = addTask(String(args.text), priority)?.id ?? null;
},
```

## One declaration can sit on a component

The search field is a custom component with one input inside it. The component exists to wrap the field with an icon and to own the Enter behavior:

```tsx{6,15-19}
export const SearchBox = forwardRef<HTMLDivElement, SearchBoxProps>(function SearchBox(
  { value, label, placeholder, onChange, onSearch },
  ref,
) {
  return (
    <div className="search-box" ref={ref}>
      <span className="search-box__icon" aria-hidden="true">⌕</span>
      <input
        type="search"
        aria-label={label}
        autoComplete="off"
        placeholder={placeholder}
        value={value}
        onChange={(event) => onChange(event.target.value)}
        onKeyDown={(event) => {
          if (event.key !== "Enter") return;
          event.preventDefault();
          onSearch();
        }}
      />
    </div>
  );
});
```

The declarations belong to the wrapper, not to the input:

```tsx{1-12,14-17}
const searchTextRef = usePlingTool<HTMLDivElement>({
  id: "search_text",
  desc: copy.searchTextDesc,
  kind: "write",
  action: "fill",
});
const searchEnterRef = usePlingTool<HTMLDivElement>({
  id: "search_enter",
  desc: copy.searchEnterDesc,
  kind: "write",
  action: "press",
  key: "Enter",
});

const searchRef = useMemo(
  () => mergeRefs(searchTextRef, searchEnterRef),
  [searchEnterRef, searchTextRef],
);
```

The React option is `action: "fill"`; the adapter projects that as the `type` primitive. The tool list shows the primitive; the activity row shows the action id, not the primitive name. `mergeRefs` then lets both declarations attach to the same DOM node. Each action still has its own id, primitive, and description. The framework searches inside the wrapper and finds exactly one compatible input. That result is reported as fidelity `auto`: there is one defensible candidate, but the component's behavior, not the framework, decides what the input means.

The two actions are not an accident of the example. The page itself separates writing from applying: typing into the field does not change the visible list, and pressing Enter does. Keeping `search_text` and `search_enter` separate preserves that behavior and makes the second step visible in the run record.

## Several controls require an explicit target

`TaskFilters` contains three buttons. All three use the same primitive, and automatic lookup has no non-arbitrary way to choose one. Attaching one declaration to the component root would therefore be ambiguous.

Each action names its button:

```tsx{1-8,10-17,19-26}
const showAllRef = usePlingTool<HTMLDivElement>({
  id: "show_all_tasks",
  desc: copy.showAllDesc,
  kind: "read",
  action: "click",
  target: 'button[data-filter="all"]',
});
const showOpenRef = usePlingTool<HTMLDivElement>({
  id: "show_open_tasks",
  desc: copy.showOpenDesc,
  kind: "read",
  action: "click",
  target: 'button[data-filter="active"]',
});
const showCompletedRef = usePlingTool<HTMLDivElement>({
  id: "show_completed_tasks",
  desc: copy.showCompletedDesc,
  kind: "read",
  action: "click",
  target: 'button[data-filter="completed"]',
});

const filtersRef = useMemo(
  () => mergeRefs(showAllRef, showOpenRef, showCompletedRef),
  [showAllRef, showCompletedRef, showOpenRef],
);
```

The target is a CSS selector inside the declaration element, not a search of the whole document. That boundary matters. It keeps an action tied to the component the developer declared, and it prevents a later part of the page from satisfying the selector by accident.

An explicit target raises fidelity to `high` with the reason `declared` only when it matches exactly one element inside the declaration element. If it matches nothing, the action remains registered but resolves to `low` with `target-missing`. The selector is a claim about the component's structure, not a permission check, and it does not prove that the click produced the intended business result.

## Hover can reveal the next target

The bulk menu is closed by default. Its clear button does not exist in the DOM until the menu opens. Because `clear_completed` is declared on that button, no binding exists while the menu is closed: the action is absent from the registry, not merely unavailable. A declaration on the always-mounted wrapper with a target selector would behave differently. It would still be registered, but would resolve to `low` with `target-missing` while the button is absent.

The page opens the menu on pointer entry:

```tsx{10-12,24-29}
export const BulkMenu = forwardRef<HTMLDivElement, BulkMenuProps>(function BulkMenu(
  { label, clearLabel, clearRef, completed, onClear },
  ref,
) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

  return (
    <div
      className="bulk"
      ref={ref}
      onMouseOver={() => setOpen(true)}
      onMouseLeave={() => setOpen(false)}
    >
      <button
        className="bulk__trigger"
        type="button"
        aria-expanded={open}
        onClick={() => setOpen((current) => !current)}
      >
        {label}
      </button>
      {open ? (
        <div className="bulk__menu">
          <button
            ref={clearRef}
            className="todo__clear"
            type="button"
            disabled={completed === 0}
            onClick={onClear}
          >
            {clearLabel}
          </button>
        </div>
      ) : null}
    </div>
  );
});
```

The two declarations attach to different elements:

```tsx{1-12}
const openBulkMenuRef = usePlingTool<HTMLDivElement>({
  id: "open_bulk_menu",
  desc: copy.openBulkMenuDesc,
  kind: "read",
  action: "hover",
  fidelity: "high",
});
const clearCompletedRef = usePlingTool<HTMLButtonElement>({
  id: "clear_completed",
  desc: copy.clearCompletedDesc,
  kind: "danger",
});
```

The hover action is declared on the always-mounted wrapper. Its `fidelity: "high"` is an explicit claim that the wrapper owns the pointer handlers. After the hover primitive runs, React renders the menu, and the clear button's own declaration enters the registry. The clear action needs no `target` because the button itself is the declaration element.

Availability and absence are different failure modes. A mounted action can be unavailable because it is disabled or covered. An action declared on an element that has not rendered is absent from the registry. An action whose declaration mounts but whose `target` is missing remains registered and resolves to `low` with `target-missing`. The model cannot call an absent action, and a registered `low` action still has no defensible DOM path.

## Fidelity is evidence, not a success flag

The fixture produces different fidelity values for different reasons:

| Value | How it was obtained | What it means here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `high`, `native` | the declaration sits on a native `<select>` or button | the element can receive the primitive directly |
| `high`, `declared` | the developer supplied `target` | there is a specific, reviewable element inside the component |
| `high`, `declared` | the developer set `fidelity: "high"` on an element that owns the event | the claim should match the component's handlers |
| `auto` | exactly one compatible input was found inside the wrapper | the DOM path is credible, but the component still owns the behavior |
| `low` | lookup was disabled, `target` matched nothing, or several candidates remained | the result must not be presented as proof that the page reacted |

A declared `target` and an explicit `fidelity` claim both report the reason `declared`; they differ in what the developer supplied. The reason explains how the target was accepted, not whether the operation succeeded.

The value never means “the business operation succeeded.” A click can reach the right button and still fail validation, hit a server error, or produce the wrong record. Conversely, a `low` result does not guarantee that the browser event had no effect. It says the framework lacked a defensible explanation for the target.

`autoTarget: false` is narrower than `run`. It stops lookup inside the declaration element. If that element handles the click itself, an explicit fidelity claim may be accurate. If it does not, the action still has no reliable DOM path and should use `run` or declare the correct target instead.

## When not to simulate the control

There are real cases where a component cannot be operated faithfully through DOM events. A canvas editor, a virtualized list that destroys rows, or a widget that maintains an internal keyboard state machine may not expose a stable element for the intended operation. In those cases, expose a small application operation with `run` and a result condition.

Do not use `run` to hide an unresolved target. If the page already has a native control with the right behavior, use it. If the component can name one internal control, use `target`. Use `run` when the interaction itself is not the contract; the business operation is.

## Next step

The page now gives the agent native controls, a single-input component, an explicitly targeted multi-button component, and content that appears only after a pointer event. Each interaction resolves to a fidelity value and a reason: `native` for a direct control, `declared` for an explicit target or fidelity claim, `auto` for one inferred candidate, and `low` when no defensible target exists. The run record surfaces non-high values; target selectors remain in the source. Each interaction stays at the page level rather than becoming an invented business shortcut.

The next chapter turns to repeated row actions. It explains how a list of records can expose one operation without producing one tool per row, and what evidence remains after an operation changes the data.

---

# Records, row actions, and change evidence

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/react/records-row-actions-and-change-evidence

The previous chapter followed each interaction down to the element that actually receives it. A list adds a problem that a single control does not expose: when many rows share the same checkbox and delete button, how does the agent know which business object it is changing, and how can the result show that the intended row changed?

Three mechanisms answer different parts of that problem. A **record** describes the data in a row. A **folded row action** turns many element-level controls into one operation with a `record` argument. **Change evidence** compares the visible page before and after execution. None of them replaces authorization, a success condition, or transactional guarantees.

The earlier chapters already used a record and the folded `toggle` action in the Todo path. This chapter makes the rules explicit, adds a second row operation with a destructive outcome, and separates what each form of evidence can and cannot prove.

## Element-level declarations multiply in a list

The Todo page now has three rows. If each row exposes a completion button and a delete button as independent actions, the model receives six row actions. A hundred rows produce two hundred. The list grows with the data, while the number of operations the user can actually request remains two.

The element ids have a second problem. `toggle@t2` may tell the framework where to dispatch an event, but it does not tell the model what `t2` means. The model can click the second checkbox without knowing that the row is “Book the design review”, that it is still open, or that the user's phrase referred to that row rather than the one above it.

The page therefore needs three things:

- a stable identity and a small data view for every row;
- one model-facing operation per kind of row action, rather than one per row;
- a result that reports observable changes to the exposed data and controls.

The business behavior stays ordinary React. The row still uses component state, the same click handlers, and the same buttons. Pling adds declarations around that behavior; it does not create a second Todo store.

## Declare what each row means

Each task already has a stable `id`, text, completion state, and priority. The row component declares a record and attaches it to the list item:

```tsx{2-8,14-18,31-39}
function TaskRow({ task, copy, onToggle, onRemove }: TaskRowProps) {
  const rowRef = usePlingRecord<HTMLLIElement>({
    data: task,
    fields: {
      text: task.text,
      status: task.done ? "completed" : "open",
      priority: copy.priorities[task.priority],
    },
  });
  const toggleRef = usePlingTool<HTMLButtonElement>({
    id: `toggle@${task.id}`,
    desc: copy.toggleDesc(task.text, task.done),
  });
  const removeRef = usePlingTool<HTMLButtonElement>({
    id: `remove@${task.id}`,
    desc: copy.removeDesc(task.text),
    kind: "danger",
  });

  return (
    <li ref={rowRef} className={task.done ? "task is-done" : "task"} data-task-id={task.id}>
      <button ref={toggleRef} type="button" className="task__check" onClick={() => onToggle(task.id)}>
        {task.done ? "✓" : ""}
      </button>
      <span className="task__body">
        <span className="task__text">{task.text}</span>
        <span className={`task__priority priority--${task.priority}`}>
          {copy.priorities[task.priority]}
        </span>
      </span>
      <button
        ref={removeRef}
        type="button"
        className="task__remove"
        aria-label={copy.deleteTaskAria(task.text)}
        onClick={() => onRemove(task.id)}
      >
        ×
      </button>
    </li>
  );
}
```

The record id comes from `task.id`, producing `t1`, `t2`, and `t3`. The model sees only the fields selected in the declaration:

```text
t1: text Review the launch checklist; status open; priority Today
t2: text Book the design review; status open; priority Soon
t3: text Send the customer follow-up; status completed; priority Later
```

`usePlingRecord(task)` is the short form. It takes the id from `task.id` or `task.key` and exposes the remaining object properties. The explicit form is used here for three reasons:

- a completion boolean is less useful than a stable `open` / `completed` value;
- the model should see the human-readable priority rather than guess what `soon` means;
- fields unrelated to the operation, including future private or derived data, do not leave the page merely because they live on the same object.

The distinction between `status` and `priority` is deliberate. `status` is a stable machine value because row actions and evidence depend on it; translating it would make the same state appear different after a locale change. `priority` is a display label selected for the current interface. If application logic also needed to compare priorities, expose the stable enum as a separate field instead of parsing the label.

The declaration registers the row; it does not copy the row into a second store. The selected fields are read from the current object when a snapshot is assembled. A completion or priority change is therefore visible on the next turn without re-registering the row. Replacing the row with a different id creates a different record.

Pling never scrapes the text inside the `<li>` to infer these fields. DOM text mixes labels, formatting, and hidden content, loses the original types, and can expose information the page never intended to publish. The declaration is the disclosure boundary for row data.

## Give each row action a stable identity

The two row actions encode both the operation and the record:

```tsx{1-5,9-10}
const toggleRef = usePlingTool<HTMLButtonElement>({
  id: `toggle@${task.id}`,
  desc: copy.toggleDesc(task.text, task.done),
});

const removeRef = usePlingTool<HTMLButtonElement>({
  id: `remove@${task.id}`,
  desc: copy.removeDesc(task.text),
  kind: "danger",
});
```

The ids are `toggle@t1`, `toggle@t2`, `remove@t1`, and so on. The text before the final `@` is the action template; the text after it is the record id. The two halves must refer to the same row that the declaration registered.

Stable ids matter more than short ids. A record based on an array index would move when the list is sorted or a row is deleted. The next action could then affect a different task while still using a syntactically valid id. The id used by the React `key`, the record, and the row actions should all come from the same durable business identifier.

The delete declaration uses `kind: "danger"`. This is a risk classification, not a style attribute. With the default approval policy, a destructive action asks for confirmation on every call and does not offer “always allow”. That gate is useful, but it is not a complete security boundary: the server must still authorize the deletion, and the application must decide whether the operation is allowed for the current user. The next chapters cover approval and sensitive data in more depth.

## Fold repeated actions into one model tool

Every element-level action remains registered as `toggle@t1`, `remove@t2`, and so on. Exact ids are needed for execution, permissions, audit, and replaying a specific call.

The model-facing projection is smaller. When at least two actions share a template and their suffixes match declared record ids, the protocol layer emits one tool per template:

```text
toggle(record)
  Mark the selected task as open or completed.
  record: one of t1 / t2 / t3

remove(record)
  Delete the selected task. This cannot be undone.
  record: one of t1 / t2 / t3
```

The count now grows with the number of operation types, not with rows times operations. A hundred rows with the same two controls still produce two folded tools.

A call such as `{ "record": "t2" }` is mapped back to the exact action `toggle@t2`. The same permission check, availability check, target resolution, and event path run as for a direct call. Folding changes the interface presented to the model, not the implementation of the operation.

Folding has two deliberate limits. One row using a template is not folded, because a direct id is shorter. A template is also not folded without record ids, because `record` must refer to data the model has actually seen. An action id alone is not treated as a source of business identity.

The distinction is visible in an audit trail. The model chooses a business record; the framework executes a precise element-level action. Logs can retain `remove@t3`, while the user-facing explanation can say “Delete *Send the customer follow-up*”.

## Record what visibly changed

A successful execution result contains more than `{ ok: true }`. The executor takes a snapshot before the action, waits for the page to settle, takes another snapshot, and compares the exposed data.

Completing `t2` produces evidence like this:

```json
{
  "changed": {
    "observed": true,
    "records": {
      "added": [],
      "removed": [],
      "updated": [{ "id": "t2", "fields": ["status"] }],
      "reordered": false,
      "omitted": { "added": 0, "removed": 0, "updated": 0 }
    }
  }
}
```

Deleting `t3` reports both the missing row and the row actions that disappeared with it:

```json
{
  "changed": {
    "observed": true,
    "records": {
      "added": [],
      "removed": ["t3"],
      "updated": [],
      "reordered": false,
      "omitted": { "added": 0, "removed": 0, "updated": 0 },
      "total": { "from": 3, "to": 2 }
    },
    "actions": {
      "added": [],
      "removed": ["toggle@t3", "remove@t3"],
      "omitted": { "added": 0, "removed": 0 }
    }
  }
}
```

Adding a task reports its new id under `records.added`. A search or filter may primarily change `actions`, because a different set of rows can now be operated on.

The payload is intentionally narrow. `updated` lists changed field names rather than copying old and new values. Added, removed, and updated collections are capped at five entries, with an `omitted` count for the remainder. That is enough to confirm the intended row changed without turning every tool result into a second copy of the page.

Evidence is captured after the adapter's settle step. React state updates and DOM commits are not instantaneous, and a target component may update on a later tick. Reading the after-snapshot too early produces false evidence, usually “no change” after a successful operation.

## Keep three guarantees separate

Records, folded actions, and diffs make an operation easier to observe, but they do not merge three different safety questions:

| Mechanism | Question it answers | What it does not prove |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Policy and approval | May this caller attempt this action? | That the page changed. |
| `expect` | Did the declared business condition become true? | Everything else that changed around it. |
| `changed` | Which exposed records, actions, state, or feedback differ between two snapshots? | That the change was complete, correct, or visible to every consumer. |

For a write, `changed.observed: false` is a warning rather than a failed action. The handler may have run without a visible effect, or it may have changed data the page does not expose. Read-only actions do not raise that warning for an empty diff, because navigation and scrolling often change no records by design.

Evidence is also not a transaction. If a handler adds and removes a row before the after-snapshot, the intermediate state is invisible. If a network request completes after the settle window, its result is outside the evidence. If the page never declares a field, the diff cannot report that field. A business invariant spanning several resources belongs in the application or server, not in a DOM comparison.

Finally, evidence does not establish intent. A diff can prove that a row changed; it cannot prove that the change is what the user asked for. The model still has to combine the user's request, the action description, the record fields, and the observed result.

## Inspect the projection and the result

Open **Activity**, then **Diagnostics**, after one delete. Three views answer different questions:

- **Records** should show one entry per task with only `text`, `status`, and `priority`. Object properties that were not declared should not appear.
- **Actions** should show the exact ids, including `toggle@t3` and `remove@t3` before the delete and the row actions that disappeared afterward.
- **Model calls** should show the folded `toggle` and `remove` tools, each with a required `record` property, rather than one tool definition per row.

For a delete, the confirmation prompt is part of the risk path, not part of the evidence. Approving it permits the attempt. The tool result and the next page snapshot are what show whether the attempt changed the page.

## Test the declarations, projection, and evidence separately

The fixture test checks three layers independently. This keeps a broken record declaration from being hidden by a model answer that happens to sound correct.

First, the registry snapshot must contain the records in page order with only the declared fields. Second, the protocol projection is built directly from that snapshot with `buildProtocol`:

```tsx
const protocol = buildProtocol(pling.registry.snapshot());

expect(protocol.templates.get("remove")).toMatchObject({
  template: "remove@",
  records: ["t1", "t2", "t3"],
});
```

The test also checks that the folded tool requires `record` and that no `toggle_t1`-style tool was emitted. Third, execution is tested against exact ids: `toggle@t2` reports `status` as updated, `remove@t3` reports the removed row and disappeared actions, and `add_task` reports the added row. A replay model then calls `toggle` and `remove` with record ids and produces the expected page state.

That division also reflects the runtime layering. Declaration answers what the page exposes. Projection answers what the model can call. Evidence answers what the executor observed. A failure in one layer should not be diagnosed as a failure in another.

## Run and verify the example

From the repository root, start the English interface:

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev r-07
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5247/`. The source is in `examples/tutorials/r-07-records-row-actions-and-change-evidence`. For Chinese, use `pnpm tutorial:dev r-07 --locale zh` and open `http://127.0.0.1:5247/?lang=zh`.

Check the following:

1. Ask the assistant to mark “Book the design review” as completed. The second row should change state and the result should report `status` updated on `t2`.
2. Ask it to delete “Send the customer follow-up”. Confirm the destructive operation. The third row should disappear, and the evidence should mention `t3` plus the row actions that disappeared with it.
3. Ask it to add “Draft the release note” with later priority. The new row should appear under `records.added`, and its record should contain the three declared fields.
4. Open **Activity** and inspect **Diagnostics**. Confirm that the record list does not include undeclared object properties and that the model saw `toggle` / `remove` rather than one tool per row.

The model may choose different wording or combine tool calls in a different order. The trace, not the prose, is the source of truth.

## Boundaries and next step

- The example has three visible rows. Record limits and off-screen rows are addressed with long lists later.
- Records are a selective view, not a security boundary. Sensitive values need explicit masking or exclusion.
- A diff compares exposed snapshots. It cannot see hidden data, server state, or work that finishes after the evidence window.
- Evidence is not transactional and does not guarantee ordering across several actions.
- Folded actions still need a faithful DOM target or a declared `run`; a record does not make an unsafe target safe.
- Stable record ids are mandatory. An index-based id can silently point at a different row after insertion, deletion, or sorting.
- `danger` starts a confirmation path; it does not replace server-side authorization or business validation.

The next chapter, [Function-level tools](/react/function-level-tools), covers operations that have no useful control to click. Records identify the object of an operation; a function-level tool is for an operation whose real contract is already a function.

---

# Function-level tools

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/react/function-level-tools

The previous chapter gave the agent a way to identify a task by record id and inspect the difference between two exposed page states. Every action still belonged to a real control: a form, a checkbox, a delete button, or a menu item.

Applications also contain operations without a matching control. A page may support marking every open task complete without offering a bulk button; the capability may exist for a mobile flow, a command-line client, or another interface and remain reachable only through code. The agent should be able to use that capability without pretending that the page contains a clickable element.

A **function-level tool** is the declaration for such an operation. Its implementation is an ordinary application function rather than a DOM interaction. It keeps the same action id, policy check, executor, and receipt shape as every other action. The only difference is that it has no target element.

## An operation without a control

The Todo example still has per-row completion, deletion, filtering, and record projection. It has no “complete all” button. The new business operation is simply to mark every open task as completed.

One possible shortcut is to add a hidden button, attach a tool to it, and let the agent click it. That moves the problem into harder-to-maintain territory:

- the action claims to operate on an element that a person cannot see or reach;
- visibility, obstruction, and scrolling rules now apply to an artificial target;
- the page gains a control that exists only for the agent, including its keyboard and accessibility surface;
- a change to the button's styling or event handling can break the tool even when the business function has not changed.

The semantic problem is more important. The model should see “complete every open task”, not “click a hidden button”. If the page does not expose that control, the capability layer should not invent it.

## Keep the existing business function

Manual interaction remains unchanged. `toggleTask`, `removeTask`, filtering, and form submission still use the original React state and event handlers. The new bulk operation changes the same `tasks` array:

```tsx{1-13}
const tasksRef = useRef(tasks);
tasksRef.current = tasks;

function completeOpenTasks(): number {
  const current = tasksRef.current;
  const openTasks = current.filter((task) => !task.done);
  const next = current.map((task) =>
    task.done ? task : { ...task, done: true }
  );
  tasksRef.current = next;
  setTasks(next);
  return openTasks.length;
}
```

The function has one job: find the open tasks, update them, and return the number that changed. It does not click anything, and it does not copy the page structure into a second state store.

The extra `tasksRef` is a React timing detail, not a framework requirement. A callback registered by a declaration can still run after a component has rendered again. If it captures one particular rendering's `tasks` array, availability and the success predicate may read stale state. The ref points at the current collection on every render; the bulk function also writes the next array into the ref before calling `setTasks`, so the success predicate can inspect the business state immediately. React and the framework's settle step still determine when the DOM commits.

## Declare the action with `useAgentTool`

Once the business function exists, register it as an action:

```tsx{1-16}
useAgentTool({
  id: "complete_open_tasks",
  desc: copy.completeOpenDesc,
  kind: "write",
  available: () =>
    tasksRef.current.some((task) => !task.done)
      ? true
      : copy.completeOpenNone,
  run: () => ({ completed: completeOpenTasks() }),
  expect: {
    desc: copy.completeOpenExpect,
    check: () => tasksRef.current.every((task) => task.done),
  },
});
```

The declaration has no `action`, `target`, or `fidelity` field. There is no element to click, fill, press, or resolve. The framework records the action with the `call` primitive. `fidelity: "high"` means the call reaches the supplied function directly; it does not mean the business result is correct.

The fields answer different questions:

| Field | Job |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Stable model-facing identity and the key used by the executor. It shares a namespace with element actions. |
| `desc` | Explains what the operation does. It matters more when there is no visible control to infer meaning from. |
| `kind` | `write` states that the operation changes application state; it is not authorization by itself. |
| `available` | Whether the operation is worth attempting in the current page state. |
| `run` | Calls the business implementation once and returns a bounded result. |
| `expect` | States what the application expects to observe after the call. |

This action takes no input, so it does not need `params`. If the operation needs an order number, a reason, or a filter, declare the argument as you would for an element action; the executor validates it before `run`. TypeScript types disappear at runtime and the model cannot read them, so an interface type alone is not enough.

## The same execution pipeline as element actions

“No element” does not mean “bypass the executor”. The framework still resolves the action by id, validates arguments, checks policy and confirmation, invokes `run`, waits for the success predicate, and compares the page before and after. A function-level tool gets no extra privilege and has no private `eval` or `click(selector)` escape hatch.

The differences are confined to element-specific steps. A function-level tool has no target to resolve, no native disabled state, and no element that can be clipped or covered by a dialog. `available` therefore becomes the main page-state check the developer can provide. It says whether the operation makes sense now; it does not perform tenant isolation, user authorization, or server-side validation.

When the component unmounts, the hook unregisters its action, so the capability list does not keep a function that no longer exists.

## One call, one observable outcome

`run` is the whole business call:

```tsx
run: () => ({ completed: completeOpenTasks() })
```

It does not fill a hidden input or dispatch a synthetic click. The task collection is updated directly, and the return value keeps only a count. That value becomes `data` in the execution result. Counts, short ids, and confirmations belong there; the whole task list or a full external response does not.

The success criterion belongs in `expect`:

```tsx
expect: {
  desc: copy.completeOpenExpect,
  check: () => tasksRef.current.every((task) => task.done),
}
```

The framework waits for that condition after `run`. When it holds, the receipt carries “No task remains open”; when it times out, the result is `EXPECTATION_FAILED`. That distinction separates “the function returned” from “the application reached the expected state”.

In React, do not write `expect` against a value captured by one render, and do not substitute the current filtered rows for the business state. The first may never observe the new array; the second proves only that visible rows are complete, not that every task is complete.

An example receipt looks like this:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "action": {
    "id": "complete_open_tasks",
    "description": "Mark every open task as completed. This changes all open records in one operation."
  },
  "expect": "No task remains open",
  "data": { "completed": 2 },
  "changed": {
    "observed": true,
    "records": {
      "added": [],
      "removed": [],
      "updated": [
        { "id": "t1", "fields": ["status"] },
        { "id": "t2", "fields": ["status"] }
      ],
      "reordered": false
    }
  }
}
```

The three layers have different uses:

- `data` is the business summary returned by the function;
- `expect` is the success condition the framework actually observed;
- `changed` is the difference between exposed records across the execution.

None of them is a server transaction receipt. If the task collection is later synchronized over the network, local state may succeed and the server may still reject the write. An application must expose a separate server acknowledgement when remote correctness matters. The change summary is also limited to declared fields; it cannot prove what happened in a database, an email service, or an audit log.

## Choosing a declaration form

The React adapter offers three forms for different situations:

| Declaration | Use it when | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `usePlingTool` with a native interaction | A real control receives the interaction and its native behavior is reliable. | The action is bound to an element and participates in target resolution, visibility, and obstruction rules. |
| `usePlingTool` with `run` | A real control exists, but reproducing its DOM interaction would be unreliable or would split one business operation into several steps. | The action remains element-bound; the injected path performs the business function directly. |
| `useAgentTool` | The operation already exists as application logic, but no control should represent it. | There is no target, visibility check, or hover highlight. Availability is entirely declared by the developer. |

Do not use a function-level tool merely to avoid writing a clear control declaration. When a real button owns the operation, declaring that button is usually easier to understand and easier to keep aligned with what the user sees. Use the function-level form when the absence of a control reflects the product.

Compound behavior such as opening a dialog, filling several fields, and saving should be composed as a flow rather than hidden inside an opaque function. One function-level tool should represent one understandable business operation.

## Common mistakes

| Symptom | Cause | Better response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The tool remains present when the operation is not possible | No `available` predicate, or a check of component mounting only | Check the business precondition and return a readable reason. |
| The call succeeds but its result cannot be confirmed | The function returns before the page settles, or the affected fields are not exposed | Add `expect`, expose the relevant fields, and wait for React to render. |
| A filter makes the page look fully complete | The success predicate checks the visible DOM instead of the business state | Read the current task collection, not the current list view. |
| A bulk operation makes the context grow | `run` returns every object or a complete external response | Return a count, ids, or a bounded summary. |
| `kind` is treated as permission | `write` or `danger` is assumed to decide who may call the action | Keep policy, confirmation, and server-side authorization independent. |
| A hook is called after an early return | `useAgentTool` is not at the component's top level | Keep the hook at the top level so registration follows the component lifecycle. |

The framework rejects a missing `desc`, rejects duplicate action ids, and keeps unavailable actions visible with their reason. It does not decide the business policy, and it does not treat a function result as proof that an external system accepted the change.

## Verify the example

From the repository root, start the English example:

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev r-08
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5248/`. For the Chinese interface, use `pnpm tutorial:dev r-08 --locale zh` and `http://127.0.0.1:5248/?lang=zh`. The example source is in `examples/tutorials/r-08-function-level-tools`.

Check these paths:

1. Ask the assistant: `Mark every open task as completed.` The two open rows should become complete, with their record fields and visible checked state updated together.
2. Open **Activity**, then **Diagnostics**. The `complete_open_tasks` receipt should include `completed: 2`, the expectation `No task remains open`, and updates for `t1` and `t2`.
3. Ask again. The action should remain in the capability list with the declared unavailable reason instead of running a second time.
4. Reload the page, then add, complete, and delete tasks manually. Confirm that the form, checkboxes, delete buttons, and filters still behave as before.
5. Ask the assistant to add a task, then complete every open task. The new task should participate in the same record diff.
6. Inspect the tool list in diagnostics. `complete_open_tasks` should have no element target and should not be folded into a record template.

## Scope and next step

A function-level tool solves the problem of an operation without a control. It does not solve the problem of whether a control is visible. While mounted and available, the tool always exists; it has no target that can be scrolled out of view, clipped by a parent, or covered by a dialog. It is not a way to bypass the visibility rules that apply to real controls.

The next chapter returns to the element layer. It covers regions, visibility, and overlays: how a page tells the agent which area is active, which controls are clipped or covered, and which actions remain valid after a dialog opens.

Next: [Regions, visibility, and overlays](/react/regions-visibility-and-overlays).

# Regions, visibility, and overlays

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/react/regions-visibility-and-overlays

The previous chapters gave actions stable identities and descriptions, and gave repeated row operations a record argument. The model no longer has to infer an operation from element order alone.

That is still not enough when several parts of a page contain similar controls, or when a dialog temporarily makes the rest of the page unusable. A flat action list cannot say which **Save** belongs to the task editor and which belongs to a settings form. It also cannot explain why an operation that existed a moment ago is absent from the current list.

This chapter adds two kinds of context:

- **regions** describe where an action belongs in the page structure;
- **availability** says that an action still exists but cannot be used right now, and why.

The example is a real task editor in the Todo application. It changes the task, and it makes the background page inert while it is open. Neither mechanism grants permission or replaces business validation.

## Why a flat action list is ambiguous

Consider two operations with similar purposes in different parts of an application:

```text
save              Save the current record.
save              Save the account settings.
```

Better names and descriptions help, but they do not solve the underlying problem: the model does not know which part of the page each operation belongs to. A person reads the page spatially. The model receives a list.

The Todo page shows the same problem on a smaller scale. It has an add form, a task list, filters, and bulk controls. The add action belongs to the composer, row actions belong to records, and filters belong to the view toolbar. Names are usually enough on a page this small, but structure becomes necessary as controls repeat.

An overlay adds a second problem. While the editor is open, the task list is covered and should not accept interaction. If those actions simply disappear from the snapshot, the model can reasonably conclude that the page no longer has an add form or row actions. It needs the weaker and more accurate statement: the actions still exist, but the open editor prevents their use.

The goal is therefore not to expose more controls. It is to make the existing page model more faithful:

1. actions carry a readable region path;
2. a dialog belongs to the page tree even when React renders it outside that tree with a portal;
3. covered controls remain present as unavailable, with a reason;
4. actions without a target element declare their availability explicitly.

The business functions and data model remain unchanged. This chapter adds region declarations, dialog semantics, and one availability condition.

## Describe the page as a small tree

The Todo workspace already has one region. This chapter makes its internal structure explicit:

```tsx{1-24,27-30}
const todoScope = usePlingScope<HTMLElement>({
  id: "todo",
  label: "Tasks",
  description: "The task workspace: adding, editing, filtering, and reviewing tasks.",
  role: "main",
});
const composerScope = usePlingScope<HTMLFormElement>({
  id: "composer",
  label: "Task composer",
  description: "Create a task and choose its priority.",
  role: "form",
});
const taskListScope = usePlingScope<HTMLUListElement>({
  id: "task_list",
  label: "Task list",
  description: "Visible tasks with completion, edit, and delete actions.",
  role: "list",
});
const viewControlsScope = usePlingScope<HTMLElement>({
  id: "view_controls",
  label: "View controls",
  description: "Filtering and bulk operations for the task list.",
  role: "toolbar",
});

return (
  <section ref={todoScope}>
    <form ref={composerScope}>{/* Composer controls */}</form>
    <ul ref={taskListScope}>{/* Task rows */}</ul>
    <footer ref={viewControlsScope}>{/* Filters and bulk actions */}</footer>
  </section>
);
```

`usePlingScope` returns a callback ref. Mounting the corresponding element adds the region to the page model; unmounting it removes the region. A child region normally inherits the nearest ancestor region from the DOM.

The model receives a tree similar to:

```text
## Page structure (regions)
- main "Tasks" (todo): ...
  - form "Task composer" (composer): ...
  - list "Task list" (task_list): ...
  - toolbar "View controls" (view_controls): ...
```

Actions inherit the path of the region in which they are declared. The add action therefore carries `region:Tasks / Task composer`; an edit or delete action carries `region:Tasks / Task list`; a filter action carries `region:Tasks / View controls`.

This path helps even when descriptions are similar. It gives the model a stable way to distinguish operations without inspecting CSS or guessing from DOM order.

`role` is a structural hint. The supported values are `page`, `header`, `nav`, `main`, `aside`, `section`, `form`, `dialog`, `toolbar`, `list`, and `footer`. It affects the page description and reading order, but it does not expose controls, grant access, or validate an operation.

## Put the dialog back into the page tree

The editor is rendered to `document.body` with `createPortal`, so it is not a DOM descendant of the Todo workspace:

```tsx{1-8,13-20}
const editDialogScope = usePlingScope<HTMLDivElement>({
  id: "edit_dialog",
  label: "Edit task",
  description: "Rename one task. The rest of the task page is inactive while this dialog is open.",
  role: "dialog",
  parent: "todo",
});

return (
  <section ref={todoScope}>
    {/* Task workspace */}
  </section>
  {editingTask ? createPortal(
    <div className="overlay" ref={editDialogScope}>
      <section role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="edit-task-title">
        {/* Editor fields and actions */}
      </section>
    </div>,
    document.body,
  ) : null}
);
```

The fixed overlay covers the page visually, but its DOM ancestry does not make it a child of the task workspace. `parent: "todo"` supplies the missing page relationship. In the model's region tree, the dialog appears under the task workspace while remaining outside that element in the browser.

The native `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"` attributes describe the widget to assistive technology. They do not create a framework-level modal boundary. The dialog enters the page model because it has a scope declaration. The background becomes unavailable because its interaction state changes, not because the DOM contains the word `dialog`.

The editor exposes only the operations needed to rename one task. Because portal content has no DOM ancestor with a scope, each action names its scope explicitly:

```tsx{1-7,9-15,17-22}
const editTextRef = usePlingTool<HTMLInputElement>({
  id: "edit_note",
  desc: "Replace the text of the task currently being edited.",
  kind: "write",
  action: "fill",
  scope: "edit_dialog",
});

const editSaveRef = usePlingTool<HTMLButtonElement>({
  id: "edit_save",
  desc: "Save the task text and close the editor.",
  kind: "write",
  scope: "edit_dialog",
  run: saveEdit,
});

const editCancelRef = usePlingTool<HTMLButtonElement>({
  id: "edit_cancel",
  desc: "Close the editor without changing the task.",
  kind: "read",
  scope: "edit_dialog",
});
```

`edit_note` and `edit_save` are separate operations because they represent two distinct user decisions. Entering text does not save it. This separation also makes a failed call understandable: the model can report that it filled the field but that saving did not complete.

`edit_save` still has a target button, so the normal element checks apply. When the input is empty, the native Save button is disabled and the operation is reported as unavailable. No extra `available` predicate is needed for that condition.

## Make the background unavailable, not absent

An overlay may cover a page visually while leaving its controls reachable by keyboard or assistive technology. The Todo workspace therefore becomes inert for as long as the editor exists:

```tsx{3-4}
<section
  className="todo"
  ref={todoScope}
  inert={editingTask ? true : undefined}
  aria-hidden={editingTask ? "true" : undefined}
>
  {/* Task workspace */}
</section>
```

`inert` is the primary interaction boundary. In a supporting browser, content inside an inert subtree cannot be focused, clicked, or reached through sequential keyboard navigation. `aria-hidden="true"` removes the same background from the accessibility tree. The two attributes are complementary; neither replaces the other.

Before reporting an element-bound action as usable, the framework checks inert ancestors as well as native `disabled`, `hidden`, `display: none`, and `visibility: hidden`. It also performs geometry checks for clipping and obstruction in a browser. The exact combination depends on the page. The important rule is that hiding a control must not be implemented by deleting its declaration.

With the editor open, the dialog actions remain available. Background actions move to a separate section:

```text
## Actions that exist but are unavailable right now
- add_task: Element is inside an inert subtree: <form class="composer"> ... | region: Tasks / Task composer
- toggle@t1: Element is inside an inert subtree: <section class="todo"> ... | region: Tasks / Task list
- show_all_tasks: Element is inside an inert subtree: <section class="todo"> ... | region: Tasks / View controls
```

Repeated row actions are deduplicated by kind, so the model does not receive one identical reason for every task. It receives the more useful fact that this class of action exists and is currently blocked.

The unavailable section is not an invitation to retry. If the model invokes `add_task` by its exact id while the dialog is open, the executor rejects the call with `ACTION_UNAVAILABLE`. Page event handlers cannot run around the page's current interaction state.

This distinction helps the model recover. It can say that the composer is unavailable while the editor is open, then save or cancel the editor before trying again. It does not need to invent a missing feature or reload the page.

## Function-level tools need an explicit guard

The bulk operation from the previous chapter has no element target. `inert` on the Todo section therefore cannot disable it. If it remained available during editing, the model could modify the whole list while the user was editing one row.

The function-level declaration must carry the page-state condition itself:

```tsx{5-12}
useAgentTool({
  id: "complete_open_tasks",
  desc: copy.completeOpenDesc,
  kind: "write",
  available: () =>
    editingIdRef.current !== null
      ? copy.editOpenBlocked
      : tasksRef.current.some((task) => !task.done)
        ? true
        : copy.completeOpenNone,
  run: () => ({ completed: completeOpenTasks() }),
});
```

The first branch is not a copy of the `inert` check. It is the missing business fact for an operation that has no DOM target. The later branches handle an empty list. Each failure returns a condition the model can act on.

The guard reads refs so that an execution step observes the latest task and dialog state, including immediately after opening or closing the editor. This is a correctness detail, not an alternative to React state.

This is the general rule for function-level tools: a tool without an element does not inherit visibility, obstruction, native disabled state, or an inert ancestor. The developer must decide which page conditions make the operation meaningful and express them through `available`. A function that can still be invoked in an invalid state also needs a runtime guard.

`available` remains a statement about the page, not authorization. It can say that the editor is open, a selection is empty, or a list is full. It cannot establish that the caller may mutate the record, that the tenant owns the data, or that a server-side rule permits the operation.

## What the model receives

The page context now has three useful layers. The region section describes the workspace and the open dialog:

```text
## Page structure (regions)
- main "Tasks" (todo): ...
  - form "Task composer" (composer): ...
  - list "Task list" (task_list): ...
  - toolbar "View controls" (view_controls): ...
  - dialog "Edit task" (edit_dialog): ...
```

The available action list contains the dialog operations and omits the blocked background actions. The next section, headed `## Actions that exist but are unavailable right now`, gives the relevant reasons. Task records remain readable, so the model can identify which task is being edited and what its current text is.

The folded `edit` row-action template disappears while the dialog is open, because every element that would implement it is unavailable. It returns when the dialog closes. This is a property of the current action projection, not a deletion of the declarations or a change to the stored records.

After `edit_save`, the next turn receives a fresh snapshot. The dialog is gone, the task record contains the new text, and the background actions are available again. The model does not need to remember that the dialog was open; the snapshot is the current source of truth.

## What visibility does not mean

Regions and availability make the page model more faithful, but they do not make the application secure by themselves:

| Fact | What it establishes | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Region membership | Which part of the declared page contains the action. | Who may invoke it. |
| `inert` or a covered target | The browser cannot use that control through the normal path at this moment. | That the business operation is valid or authorized. |
| `available` | The developer says the page state permits an attempt. | That the caller has permission, or that a server will accept the result. |
| A successful UI action | The declared implementation ran and the page settled. | That a remote write succeeded or that policy was enforced. |

A region label is not a validation rule. Renaming a region, nesting it under a dialog, or marking it active does not alter the executor's permission model. The action still passes through policy, argument validation, confirmation, and whatever authorization the application implements.

Geometry checks are local and temporary. They answer whether a control appears reachable to this browser at this moment. They cannot prove that the control matches the user's intent, and a malicious page or extension can always change the DOM. Server-side authorization and business validation remain necessary wherever the operation is consequential.

Finally, `aria-hidden` is not a universal way to make a control safe. Hiding a focusable subtree from assistive technology without making it inert can leave keyboard users in an invisible interaction state. In a modal, use the platform's interaction boundary and keep the background's semantics consistent with its actual behavior.

## Failures worth designing for

| Symptom | Cause | Better response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A dialog is labelled `dialog`, but background actions remain available | The role was mistaken for a modal boundary | Make the background truly unavailable and verify it in the snapshot. |
| The dialog appears as a second root region | It is rendered through a portal and has no explicit parent | Declare the intended parent id. |
| The model says the composer disappeared while a dialog is open | Unavailable actions were removed from both the available and unavailable lists | Keep the action present with a readable reason. |
| The bulk function still runs while a dialog is open | A function-level tool cannot inherit `inert` from a target | Add the page-state condition to `available` and keep a runtime guard. |
| Similar controls are still chosen incorrectly | Regions exist, but actions have no readable path | Give regions stable ids, labels, and descriptions that reflect their role. |
| The action is blocked, but the user sees no next step | The reason describes an implementation detail | State the condition in user-facing terms, such as “Finish or cancel the open task editor.” |

These are page-model errors. Find them in tests and by inspecting the runtime snapshot rather than leaving the interpretation to a model's prose.


## Scope and next step

This chapter covers structural regions, explicit parentage for overlays, and the difference between an action being absent and temporarily unavailable. It does not yet address long lists, scrolling, offscreen record actions, or the discovery actions generated for content outside the viewport. Those are the subject of the next chapter.

Nor does this chapter turn page state into authorization. A correct region tree tells the model where it is. A correct unavailable reason tells it what must change. Neither replaces policy, consent, or server-side validation.
