# Quick start: add Pling to a vanilla page

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/quick-start-add-pling-to-a-vanilla-page

This chapter attaches an agent to a Todo page written with ordinary DOM APIs. There is no component tree to hook into and no reactive store to expose. The page already knows how to render rows, fill a draft value, submit the form, and toggle completion. Pling adds the declarations that make those facts usable by a model.

The result is deliberately narrow. The agent can add a task and change the completion state of an existing task. It cannot delete, filter, or operate a control the page did not declare.

## What “first task” means without a framework

Consider:

> Mark the first task as completed and add “Prepare tomorrow's agenda”.

The DOM can tell a browser that three `li` elements exist. It does not tell a model which one is first in the business list, what text each contains, or whether a row is already complete. The page must declare those facts.

| Need | Vanilla declaration |
| --- | --- |
| The Todo module | `pling.scope(todo, { id: "todo", ... })` |
| Each task row | `pling.record(row, { data: task, ... })` |
| The new-task field | `pling.tool(input, { id: "composer_text", action: "fill", ... })` |
| The submit button | `pling.tool(submit, { id: "composer_submit", ... })` |
| A row's completion button | `pling.tool(check, { id: `toggle@${task.id}`, ... })` |

The record id comes from the stable task id, not from the visual position in the DOM. The model can choose `t2`; Pling resolves the matching element-level action.

## Keep the DOM and handlers

The page still creates its own markup and attaches its own events:

```ts
const form = document.querySelector<HTMLFormElement>("[data-composer]")!;
const input = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("[data-new-task]")!;
const submit = document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>("[data-submit]")!;

function addTask(): void {
  const text = input.value.trim();
  if (!text) return;
  const task = { id: `t${++sequence}`, text, done: false };
  tasks.unshift(task);
  list.prepend(renderRow(task));
  input.value = "";
  syncSummary();
}

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  addTask();
});
```

The declarations below do not replace `addTask`, `renderRow`, or the click handler. They only tell the agent where those operations live.

## Declare the region

```ts{3-8}
const todo = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>("[data-todo]")!;

const offScope = pling.scope(todo, {
  id: "todo",
  label: copy.regionLabel,
  description: copy.regionDescription,
  role: "main",
});
```

The scope gives all controls inside the Todo module a shared context. The return value is the unsubscribe function; keep it with the page's cleanup list.

## Declare the input and submit button

```ts{1-10,12-17}
const offText = pling.tool(input, {
  id: "composer_text",
  desc: copy.composerTextDesc,
  action: "fill",
  params: [{ name: "text", label: copy.textParamLabel }],
});

const offSubmit = pling.tool(submit, {
  id: "composer_submit",
  desc: copy.composerSubmitDesc,
  available: () => input.value.trim() ? true : copy.submitReason,
});
```

`action: "fill"` is important. A text input is not a click target in the business sense; it accepts a value. The tool's parameters describe that value to the model.

The submit action is initially unavailable because the input is empty. After a fill, the page updates `input.value`, the availability check becomes true, and the action appears. This is the same rule a person encounters through the disabled button.

## Declare each row and its completion control

The row renderer receives a task and creates the row DOM. Attach a record and a tool while the row is created:

```ts{4,11-14,18}
function mountRow(task: Task): HTMLLIElement {
  const row = document.createElement("li");
  const check = document.createElement("button");
  const text = document.createElement("span");

  row.append(check, text);
  text.textContent = task.text;

  const offRecord = pling.record(row, {
    data: task,
    label: copy.recordLabel(task.text),
  });

  const offToggle = pling.tool(check, {
    id: `toggle@${task.id}`,
    desc: copy.toggleDesc(task.text),
  });

  check.addEventListener("click", () => {
    task.done = !task.done;
    syncRow();
    syncSummary();
  });

  return row;
}
```

The record's `data` object includes `id`, `text`, and `done`. The model can therefore read the row before choosing an operation. The tool id includes `task.id`, so two rows do not share the same control identity.

The completion description is intentionally stable: it says the control changes the completion state. The current state belongs in the record, not in a sentence that becomes stale after the click. This also avoids unbinding and rebinding the tool on every visual update.

If a row is ever removed, call `offRecord()` and `offToggle()` before discarding the element. The tutorial fixture does not remove rows, but dynamic lists are covered later.

## Mount the assistant

```ts
const dock = pling.dock({
  title: copy.dockTitle,
  quick: copy.quick,
});
```

The dock is a shared DOM surface. It uses the same registry and agent runtime as the page controls. The quick prompts are text suggestions, not hidden capabilities.

## Teardown is part of the integration

The fixture keeps every unsubscribe function in a list:

```ts
const cleanups: Array<() => void> = [];
cleanups.push(offScope, offText, offSubmit, offRecord, offToggle);

return {
  destroy() {
    for (const cleanup of cleanups.reverse()) cleanup();
    dock.destroy();
    pling.destroy();
  },
};
```

This is not ceremony. A DOM adapter cannot infer when your code discards a node. Explicit cleanup prevents the registry from describing a control that no longer exists.

## Run and verify

From the repository root:

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-03
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5241/`. For Chinese, run `pnpm tutorial:dev j-03 --locale zh` and open `http://127.0.0.1:5241/?lang=zh`.

Check:

1. Ask: `Add “Reply to the customer” to my tasks.` The task appears once.
2. Open the activity view. The run should show the input fill and the existing form submission.
3. Toggle the second row through the assistant. Only that row changes state.
4. Ask it to delete or filter. Those capabilities are not present.
5. Reload and confirm the page still behaves normally without the assistant.

## Common failures

| Symptom | Likely cause | Correction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The model sees an input but cannot submit | The submit action is still unavailable | Ensure the fill updates the real input and the availability function reads that value |
| Clicking on the row does not change the task | The declared element is not the button with the click handler | Pass the actual interactive element to `pling.tool` |
| Two rows share a control | The action id omits the stable task id | Use the id in both the record and the action |
| A removed row remains in the snapshot | The unsubscribe functions were not called | Tie registration and cleanup to the row lifecycle |
| The assistant cannot see filters | Filters were not declared | Expected; declare them only when needed |
| The page keeps working but the agent cannot see it | The declaration is attached after the element is replaced | Attach declarations to the final DOM node and re-register after replacement |

Continue with the data-attribute and dynamic-DOM chapters when they become available.

---

# Declarative actions with data attributes

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/declarative-actions-with-data-attributes

A server-rendered or template-driven page may have most of its capability metadata in HTML. Repeating a long `pling.tool()` call next to every control makes that metadata harder to inspect. A page can instead store the serializable parts in `data-*` attributes and use a small binder to call the adapter.

The Vanilla adapter does not automatically interpret `data-pling-tool`. `data-agent-*` in this chapter is an application convention. Keeping the binder in application code makes the convention visible and lets the page decide which dynamic values it needs.

## Put stable metadata in markup

The input and submit button describe their action with attributes:

```html
<input data-new-task
  data-agent-tool="composer_text"
  data-agent-desc="Enter the text for a new task."
  data-agent-action="fill"
  data-agent-params='[{"name":"text","label":"Task text"}]' />

<button type="submit" data-submit
  data-agent-tool="composer_submit"
  data-agent-desc="Add the text in the new-task field to the list.">
  Add task
</button>
```

The values are stable, readable at the point where the control is rendered, and can be produced by a server template without shipping component code. The `params` value is JSON because it is data, not executable code.

## Bind attributes after the DOM exists

The page owns a binder that turns those attributes into declarations:

```ts
function bindDataTools(root: ParentNode): void {
  for (const element of root.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>("[data-agent-tool]")) {
    const id = element.dataset.agentTool?.trim();
    const desc = element.dataset.agentDesc?.trim();
    if (!id || !desc) continue;

    const action = element.dataset.agentAction as ToolOptions["action"] | undefined;
    const rawParams = element.dataset.agentParams;
    const params = rawParams ? JSON.parse(rawParams) : undefined;
    const available = availability[id];

    cleanups.push(pling.tool(element, {
      id,
      desc,
      ...(action ? { action } : {}),
      ...(params ? { params } : {}),
      ...(available ? { available } : {}),
    }));
  }
}
```

Register the scope before binding its children. The adapter writes `data-plling-scope` to the region, and each tool inherits the nearest declared scope from the DOM.

## Keep functions and live objects in code

Two things should not be serialized into HTML:

- a record's `data` object, because it must remain the same live object the page mutates;
- an `available` function, because it reads current page state.

The page keeps an availability map and binds each row's record explicitly:

```ts
const availability = {
  composer_submit: () => input.value.trim() ? true : "Fill in a task first.",
};

pling.record(row, { data: task, label: `Task: ${task.text}` });
```

For generated rows, the page can set `data-agent-tool` and `data-agent-desc` before calling the same binder. The record and its live object remain attached with `pling.record`.

## Data attributes are metadata, not security

Anyone can inspect or alter a data attribute in the browser. The resulting declaration still goes through the same registry, availability check, policy, executor, and server authorization as an explicit `pling.tool()` call. Removing an attribute can reduce what the agent sees, but adding one cannot grant authority the business endpoint did not already allow.

Do not store secrets, access tokens, or per-user permission claims in these attributes. The browser is the wrong trust boundary for them.

## Run the example

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-04
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5269/`. The Chinese interface is available with `pnpm tutorial:dev j-04 --locale zh` at `http://127.0.0.1:5269/?lang=zh`.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-04
```

The check confirms that the attribute binder registers the input, submit, and row actions, and that the existing DOM handlers still add and toggle tasks.

## Common failures

**Putting `data-agent-tool` on every wrapper.** The binder sees every matched element. Put the metadata on the interactive control or use an explicit selector in the binder.

**Leaving stale attributes on a replaced node.** The attribute is not a registration. Re-run the binder after replacing the DOM, and call the old declaration's unsubscribe function.

**Serializing `available` or a live record into JSON.** They are code and state, not static metadata. Keep them in the page and merge them in the binder.

Next: [Imperative actions for dynamic DOM](/vanilla/imperative-actions-for-dynamic-dom).

# Imperative actions for dynamic DOM

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/imperative-actions-for-dynamic-dom

A browser page replaces nodes all the time: a row is deleted, a table is refreshed, a dialog is rebuilt, or a list is rendered from a new server response. In a component adapter, the component lifecycle normally tells the adapter when to unbind. In a plain DOM application, that lifecycle belongs to your code.

The Vanilla adapter therefore returns an unsubscribe function from every `pling.scope()`, `pling.record()`, and `pling.tool()` call. The page must keep those functions with the node they describe.

## Give every row its own declaration set

The example keeps a map from task id to the row and its cleanup functions:

```ts
const rows = new Map<string, { element: HTMLLIElement; cleanups: Array<() => void> }>();

function mountRow(task: Task): HTMLLIElement {
  const row = document.createElement("li");
  const check = document.createElement("button");
  const remove = document.createElement("button");

  const rowCleanups = [
    pling.record(row, { data: task, label: `Task: ${task.text}` }),
    pling.tool(check, { id: `toggle@${task.id}`, desc: copy.toggleDesc(task.text) }),
    pling.tool(remove, { id: `remove@${task.id}`, desc: copy.removeDesc(task.text), kind: "danger" }),
  ];

  rows.set(task.id, { element: row, cleanups: rowCleanups });
  list.append(row);
  return row;
}
```

The declaration is tied to the row's stable business id. The DOM node is not used as the identity of the task.

## Remove the declarations before the node

Removing a row must clean up its record and actions before the element disappears:

```ts
function removeTask(id: string): void {
  const entry = rows.get(id);
  if (!entry) return;

  for (const cleanup of entry.cleanups.reverse()) cleanup();
  rows.delete(id);
  entry.element.remove();
  tasks.splice(tasks.findIndex((task) => task.id === id), 1);
  syncSummary();
}
```

The order matters. If the node is removed first, the adapter can still unregister by reference, but a page that replaces a whole list without calling cleanup will leave records and actions in the registry that no user can reach. The next model turn would then see controls that no longer exist.

## Replacing the whole list

When a server response replaces every row, dispose the old row set and bind the new one:

```ts
function replaceTasks(next: Task[]): void {
  for (const entry of rows.values()) {
    for (const cleanup of entry.cleanups.reverse()) cleanup();
  }
  rows.clear();
  list.replaceChildren();
  tasks.splice(0, tasks.length, ...next);
  tasks.forEach((task) => list.append(mountRow(task)));
}
```

Do not merely assign `list.innerHTML = ...`. That destroys the old nodes without giving the page a chance to remove the old declarations. If you must use `innerHTML` as an initial render step, bind after it and keep the resulting cleanup functions.

## Why not derive actions from every button?

The adapter can optionally derive a limited set of low-confidence actions from visible controls, but it is off by default. A button with the text “Remove” does not tell the page whether it removes the current row, clears a filter, or opens a dialog. Explicit declarations keep the operation, the record, and the risk level under the application's control.

Dynamic rendering does not change that rule. Rebind an explicit declaration when the node is recreated.

## Run the example

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-05
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5270/`, or use `--locale zh` and `http://127.0.0.1:5270/?lang=zh`.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-05
```

The test removes a row through `remove@t2` and verifies that the row, its record, its toggle action, and its remove action all disappear from the registry. It also confirms that adding and toggling still work after a removal.

## Common failures

**Reusing a cleanup function for a new node.** Unsubscribing the old node does not register the new one. Keep the two operations separate.

**Storing only one cleanup per task.** A row usually has a record, several controls, and possibly a scope. Return all of them from the row's mount function.

**Using an array index as the action id.** After a deletion, the same id can refer to a different task. Use the business id.

**Forgetting the initial bind.** Dynamically generated rows and server-rendered rows both need a declaration. If the page starts with HTML, run the binder after the markup exists.

# Records and tables

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/records-and-tables

An HTML table groups cells visually. It does not tell a model which row is the same business object after a sort, which cell is its stable key, or which button changes only that row. A record adds that meaning without replacing the table.

The example keeps a semantic `<table>` and declares each `<tr>` as one task record:

```html
<table class="tasks">
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Task</th><th scope="col">Status</th><th scope="col">Complete</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody data-tasks></tbody>
</table>
```

The header explains the columns to a person. The record below explains the row to the assistant:

```ts
pling.record(row, {
  data: task,
  label: `Task: ${task.text}`,
});
```

`task` is the same object that supplies the text and status cells. If a person toggles the task, the next snapshot reads the new `done` value rather than a copy made at mount time.

## Use a stable business key

The task's id, not its row index, anchors the record and its action:

```ts
pling.tool(check, {
  id: `toggle@${task.id}`,
  desc: `Change the completion state of “${task.text}”.`,
});
```

After a sort, a filter, or an insertion, `t2` still means the same task. `row-1` would not. This is particularly important for tables because their visual order changes more often than their business identity.

## Separate the displayed cell from the record field

The status cell renders a human label such as “Open” or “Done”. The model receives the record's `done` boolean, which is the value the business logic uses. That avoids asking the model to infer state from translated text.

The table can display additional columns without exposing all of them. When a column contains sensitive data, do not put it in the record by default; mark its value explicitly with the sensitivity helpers described in the sensitive-data chapter.

## Row actions belong to the row

The completion button is inside the row and receives the stable task id. Its description identifies the exact task, while the record carries the current state. The combination lets the model choose a row and perform an operation without guessing from cell position.

Do not encode “mark complete” as a writable record field. Records are read-only. A mutation must be an action with its own availability, policy, and evidence.

## Run the example

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-06
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5271/`, or use `--locale zh` and `http://127.0.0.1:5271/?lang=zh`.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-06
```

The check confirms the table renders three records with stable ids, the row action toggles its own record, and adding a task through the form produces a fourth row with matching declarations.

## Common failures

**Putting the record on the table instead of the row.** The model then sees one large object and cannot identify which action belongs to which business item.

**Using the visible row number as the id.** Sorting and deletion break it. Use the database or business key.

**Exposing only the visible cell text.** The model may need the underlying status value, not a translated label. Keep the business value explicit and stable.

**Forgetting to remove a record when the row is destroyed.** A table refresh must clean up the old row declarations, just like any other dynamic list.

# Forms, async updates, and dialogs

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/forms-async-updates-and-dialogs

An edit form introduces two problems that a simple click does not. The dialog's controls should exist only while it is open, and a save may finish after the click has already returned. Reporting success too early gives the model a false picture of the page.

The example opens a dialog from a row action, registers its controls when it becomes visible, and waits for the saved value to appear before the save step succeeds.

## Open the dialog through the existing row action

Each row has an edit button with a stable id:

```ts
pling.tool(editButton, {
  id: `edit@${task.id}`,
  desc: `Edit “${task.text}”.`,
});
```

Clicking it runs the same `openEdit` function a person uses. That function fills the form and reveals the dialog. It does not mutate the task yet.

## Register the dialog only while it is open

The dialog begins hidden. `openEdit` declares its scope and controls at the moment it becomes visible:

```ts
dialogCleanups = [
  pling.scope(dialog, {
    id: "edit_dialog",
    label: "Edit task",
    role: "dialog",
  }),
  pling.tool(editText, {
    id: "edit_text",
    desc: "Enter the updated text for this task.",
    action: "fill",
    params: [{ name: "text", label: "Task text" }],
  }),
  pling.tool(saveButton, { id: "edit_save", desc: "Save the edited task text." }),
  pling.tool(cancelButton, { id: "edit_cancel", desc: "Close the dialog without saving." }),
];
```

`closeDialog` calls every function in reverse order before hiding the element. This is the same ownership rule as a dynamic row, applied to a temporary surface. A dialog that is hidden by CSS but remains registered is still visible to the model.

## Wait for the asynchronous result

The save button submits the form, but the page simulates persistence with a short delay:

```ts
async function saveEdit(): Promise<void> {
  const id = editingId;
  const text = editText.value.trim();
  if (!id || !text) return;

  editStatus.textContent = "Saving…";
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 80));

  const task = tasks.find((candidate) => candidate.id === id);
  if (!task) return;
  task.text = text;
  lastSaved = { id, text };
  closeDialog();
  replaceRow(task);
}
```

The tool declares an expectation, not merely a click:

```ts
expect: {
  desc: "The task text has been updated and the dialog has closed.",
  check: () => lastSaved?.id === task.id && editingId === null,
  timeout: 2_000,
}
```

The executor waits for this condition before returning a successful result. If the page shows “Saving…” forever, the model receives an expectation failure instead of a false success. This is useful for any action whose business effect arrives after the event handler returns.

## Rebind the row after the text changes

The record label and edit description contain the task text. After saving, the example replaces the row and registers it again:

```ts
function replaceRow(task: Task): void {
  const entry = rows.get(task.id);
  if (!entry) return;
  for (const cleanup of entry.cleanups.reverse()) cleanup();
  rows.delete(task.id);
  const replacement = mountRow(task, false);
  entry.element.replaceWith(replacement);
}
```

This keeps the visible label, record fields, and action descriptions consistent. If only the text node were changed, the record could still carry the old field value until the next live read.

## Run the example

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-07
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5272/`, or use `--locale zh` and `http://127.0.0.1:5272/?lang=zh`.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-07
```

The check opens `edit@t2`, verifies that dialog actions appear, fills `edit_text`, saves, waits for the asynchronous record update, and confirms that all dialog actions disappear after close.

## Common failures

**Declaring dialog actions at page startup.** They remain available after the dialog closes. Bind them in the open path and unbind them in the close path.

**Returning success immediately after the click.** The form may still be saving. Expose a result the page can check and declare it with `expect` when the wait is bounded.

**Keeping the old row record after an edit.** Rebinding the row updates labels and descriptions that contain the new value.

**Using a hidden dialog as a confirmation step.** Visibility is not approval. Destructive operations still need the confirmation policy and server-side authorization.

Next: [Mount the assistant UI](/vanilla/mount-the-assistant-ui).

# Mount the assistant UI

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/mount-the-assistant-ui

The page can provide its own entry button without creating a second assistant. `pling.dock()` returns a controller for one shared conversation; a header button simply calls that controller.

The distinction is useful when an application already has a toolbar, help menu, or keyboard shortcut. The visual entry belongs to the host page. The conversation, registry, and execution runtime remain in one place.

## Create one dock after the page exists

Create the dock after the page DOM has been rendered, then connect any host controls:

```ts
const dock = pling.dock({
  title: "Todo assistant",
  placeholder: "What needs doing?",
  emptyHint: "I can work with the task table on this page.",
  quick: ["Mark the first task as completed"],
  onOpenChange: (open) => assistantButton.setAttribute("aria-expanded", String(open)),
});

assistantButton.addEventListener("click", () => dock.toggle());
```

The button is a human entry point. It is not registered as an agent action unless the page also declares it. The dock's own launcher remains available, so the page does not have to reimplement accessibility or focus handling.

## Choose the visible options deliberately

| Option | What it changes |
| --- | --- |
| `title` | Panel heading |
| `placeholder` | Message field prompt |
| `emptyHint` | Guidance before the first turn |
| `quick` | Suggested user messages |
| `defaultOpen` | Initial panel state |
| `config` | Model or runtime overrides for this entry |
| `gate` | Confirmation channel for actions that need approval |
| `onSessionEvent` | Host-side observation of the conversation |
| `onOpenChange` | Keeps page chrome in sync with the panel |

Quick prompts are not capabilities. They are text prefilled into the normal conversation path, and the model still has to resolve a declared action.

## Keep the runtime on the page owner

A single page, route, or micro-frontend should own one Pling runtime and one dock. When the owner is destroyed, destroy the dock and then the runtime:

```ts
dock.destroy();
pling.destroy();
```

Repeated calls to `pling.dock()` create multiple entries, not multiple connections to the same panel. If the page needs a second visual affordance, call `open`, `close`, or `toggle` on the existing controller.

## Model configuration is not UI configuration

The dock can accept `config`, but a production browser should still send model requests through an authenticated gateway. The page may choose a model alias or display name; it should not embed a provider secret. Treat the dock as a client of the runtime, not as a secure model proxy.

## Run the example

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-08
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5273/`, or use `--locale zh` and `http://127.0.0.1:5273/?lang=zh`.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-08
```

The test confirms that one dock exists, the page button toggles it, and `aria-expanded` follows the opening state while the task declarations remain unchanged.

## Common failures

**Creating a dock in every component or event handler.** This creates multiple assistants. Keep one page-level controller and reuse it.

**Building a second chat panel around `pling.runtime`.** The runtime is internal to the dock integration; the public entry is the dock controller. A second panel would duplicate conversation state and accessibility behavior.

**Treating `defaultOpen` as consent.** Opening a panel is not permission to execute. Approval and server authorization remain separate.

**Forgetting to update page chrome.** Use `onOpenChange` so a custom button's label or state does not drift from the actual panel.

Next: [Sensitive data and destructive actions](/vanilla/protect-sensitive-data-and-destructive-actions).

# Protect sensitive data and destructive actions

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/protect-sensitive-data-and-destructive-actions

A support queue usually contains two kinds of risk at once. Some fields are private even though the assistant needs to work with them. Some actions change or remove data and should not follow a single click from a model without an explicit decision by the person using the page.

The example handles both cases in the same table. The model can call the account owner without receiving the phone number, and it can clear completed tasks only after the destructive action has passed the confirmation gate.

## Keep private values out of the observation

The account and note are useful context. The phone number is also necessary for one action, but sending it to the model would expose it in every request, in conversation history, and in any diagnostic transcript.

Declare each field according to what the model needs to do with it:

```ts
pling.record(row, {
  data: task,
  id: task.id,
  label: copy.recordLabel(task.text),
  fields: {
    text: task.text,
    done: task.done,
    phone: sensitive(task.phone, "token"),
    account: sensitive(task.account, {
      mode: "masked",
      mask: (value) => String(value).replace(/^(.{3}).*(.{4})$/, "$1****-$2"),
    }),
    internalNote: sensitive(task.internalNote),
  },
});
```

The three modes answer different questions:

| Mode | What the model receives | When it fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `token` | A stable reference such as <code v-pre>{{p:…}}</code> that the runtime can restore for a declared action | The model must pass the value to an operation |
| `masked` | A partial value, using the default shape or a supplied mask | A person or model needs to recognize the record without reading the full value |
| `hidden` | `[hidden]`, with the field name still present | The model only needs to know that the field exists |

`token` is not encryption. It keeps the value out of model context while allowing a declared action to use it. The runtime restores the token after argument validation and before the business function runs. A made-up token is rejected rather than passed through.

## Use the token in a narrow action

The call control accepts the phone number as an explicit parameter:

```ts
pling.tool(call, {
  id: `call@${task.id}`,
  desc: copy.callDesc(task.text),
  kind: "read",
  params: [{ name: "phone", label: copy.phoneParamLabel }],
  run: (args) => {
    lastCall = String(args.phone);
    callStatus.textContent = copy.called(lastCall.slice(-4));
  },
});
```

The model sees the token in the record and can pass the same token into `phone`. The page receives the real value only inside `run`. The visible confirmation shows the last four digits, so demonstrating the page does not reveal the full number on screen.

A token should not make an action broader than the business operation requires. Do not expose an arbitrary `dial(number)` action. Declare the specific row operation, keep its target scoped to the record, and leave authorization to the backend that owns the account.

## Treat removal as a different kind of decision

Changing a completion state is reversible. Clearing every completed task is not. The clear button therefore declares both consequences and confirmation requirements:

```ts
pling.tool(clearButton, {
  id: "clear_completed",
  desc: copy.clearDesc,
  kind: "danger",
  confirm: "always",
  available: () => tasks.some((task) => task.done)
    ? true
    : "There are no completed tasks to clear.",
  run: () => removeCompleted(),
});
```

`kind: "danger"` tells the runtime that the operation can be destructive. `confirm: "always"` prevents a session-wide approval from covering a later invocation. The action remains visible only while there is something to clear.

Confirmation is not a substitute for authorization. It records that a person approved this invocation in the page. The backend still has to check whether that person may delete the records, and whether the records may be deleted at all.

## Remove the declarations with the rows

When the clear operation removes a row, it must also remove the row's record and actions:

```ts
function removeRow(task: Task): void {
  for (const cleanup of rowCleanups.get(task.id)?.reverse() ?? []) cleanup();
  rowCleanups.delete(task.id);
  rows.get(task.id)?.remove();
  rows.delete(task.id);
}

function removeCompleted(): void {
  for (const task of tasks.filter((candidate) => candidate.done)) removeRow(task);
  for (let index = tasks.length - 1; index >= 0; index -= 1) {
    if (tasks[index]?.done) tasks.splice(index, 1);
  }
  syncSummary();
}
```

Removing only the DOM row leaves stale records and callable actions in the registry. The model would then see a task that no longer exists, or invoke a phone action whose target has already been removed.

## Run the example

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-09
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5274/`, or use `--locale zh` and `http://127.0.0.1:5274/?lang=zh`.

Ask the assistant to contact the owner of the first task. Then ask it to clear completed tasks; the destructive action should require approval. The activity view shows the declared action and its result without printing the raw phone number.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-09
```

The checks cover four boundaries: the observation contains a token, mask, and hidden value rather than the originals; the token is restored only inside the declared action; the dangerous action is always confirmed; and a denied or approved invocation produces the corresponding result.

## Common failures

**Marking every field as hidden.** The model then cannot identify the record or use the value in a permitted operation. Decide per field whether it needs the value, a partial form, or only its existence.

**Putting a sensitive value in a label or description.** Records are not the only outbound surface. Action descriptions, region descriptions, errors, and state keys must follow the same rule.

**Using `kind: "danger"` without a confirmation policy.** The risk level helps the runtime choose a policy, but an explicit `confirm` value makes the intent of a destructive operation unambiguous.

**Assuming the confirmation dialog is authorization.** It is a human decision at the page boundary. The server remains the authority for identity, scope, and business rules.

Next: [Connect vanilla pages to the model gateway](/vanilla/connect-vanilla-pages-to-the-model-gateway).

# Connect vanilla pages to the model gateway

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/connect-vanilla-pages-to-the-model-gateway

A key placed in a browser bundle is not a secret. It is sent to every visitor. Even when the variable is named `VITE_AGENT_KEY` or stored outside the repository, the built value is still readable in the page and usable by anyone who copies it.

The example removes the provider credential from the browser entirely. The page calls a same-origin endpoint. A small server process checks the session, chooses the upstream model, adds the provider key, applies limits, and returns the response.

## Keep the browser configuration ordinary

The page needs an endpoint and a model name. It does not need a provider key:

```ts
export const browserAgentConfig = {
  baseUrl: "/api/llm/v1",
  model: "server-model",
  apiKey: "",
} as const;
```

Pass that object to the page runtime:

```ts
const pling = createPling({
  agent: {
    config: {
      ...browserAgentConfig,
      systemPrompt: copy.systemPrompt,
      limits: { maxTurns: 100 },
    },
  },
});
```

The empty `apiKey` is deliberate. Cookies are sent by the browser under its normal same-origin rules, and the gateway supplies the provider credential after authenticating the request. The model name in the browser is a preference; the server can pin it or reject it.

## Authenticate before forwarding

The gateway receives a Web `Request` and returns a Web `Response`. This keeps it usable in Node, Bun, Deno, and serverless environments:

```ts
const gateway = createPlingGateway({
  upstream: {
    baseUrl: process.env.PLING_UPSTREAM_BASE_URL!,
    apiKey: process.env.PLING_UPSTREAM_API_KEY!,
  },
  model: process.env.PLING_GATEWAY_MODEL,
  allowedModels: ["server-model"],
  authorize: auth.authorize,
  allowAnonymous: false,
  onAudit(event) {
    console.log(JSON.stringify({ type: "pling.audit", ...event }));
  },
});
```

`authorize` runs before the request reaches the provider. A missing or expired session is rejected. If neither `authorize` nor `allowAnonymous: true` is configured, the gateway returns `503`; forgetting to configure authentication closes the endpoint instead of opening it.

The demo uses an HttpOnly session cookie instead of putting a token in `localStorage`. The cookie is `SameSite=Lax` and becomes `Secure` when the public origin uses HTTPS. Signing out revokes the session on the server, not merely in the page.

## Let the server choose the model

The browser may send a model name, but it should not be able to select an arbitrary or expensive one:

```ts
model: "server-model",
allowedModels: ["server-model", "server-model-fast"],
```

The gateway rejects an unknown model before calling upstream. A model picker in the page can express a preference, but it cannot grant access.

The same boundary limits request size, upstream time, and retries. These are security and availability constraints, not tuning knobs. One browser session should not be able to consume unbounded memory or upstream time.

## Record metadata, not conversations

An audit entry should answer operational questions: who called, which model, what status, how long, how many bytes, and whether retries were exhausted.

```ts
{
  type: "pling.audit",
  requestId: "…",
  user: { id: "demo-user" },
  model: "server-model",
  status: 200,
  durationMs: 842,
  bytesIn: 1780,
  bytesOut: 96,
  attempts: 1
}
```

Prompts and responses are omitted by default. They can contain customer data, personal information, or text copied from a private page. If an organization must record content for compliance, that decision needs its own retention, access, and redaction policy.

The response carries `x-pling-request-id`, so a browser failure can be matched to the server record without logging the conversation.

## Run the example

The page is a support-task table whose model route is `/api/llm/v1`. The gateway runs as a separate process.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-10
```

Copy `.env.gateway.example` to `.env.gateway`, fill in the provider settings, then start the gateway in another terminal:

```bash
pnpm --dir examples/tutorials/j-10-model-gateway dev:gateway
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5275/`, sign in with the configured demo password, and ask the assistant to work with the tasks. The browser network panel shows requests to the page origin, never to the provider and never with the provider key.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-10
```

The checks cover the browser configuration, unauthenticated rejection before upstream access, fail-closed behavior without an authorization hook, server-side key injection, model pinning, HttpOnly session cookies, revocation, and metadata-only audit records.

## Common failures

**Using a `VITE_*` variable for the provider key.** Vite embeds those values in the browser bundle. The name does not protect the value.

**Trusting the model name from the browser.** The browser can change any part of its request. Pin the model or enforce an allowlist on the server.

**Using cookies without a CSRF decision.** `SameSite=Lax` covers common cases, but cross-site forms and multiple subdomains need an explicit policy.

**Logging full prompts under “debug”.** The gateway has broad access to sensitive content. Keep operational metadata separate from content logs, and redact before data leaves the process.

**Putting the agent loop in the gateway.** In this architecture the loop remains in the page. The gateway handles transport, credentials, authentication, limits, and audit; it does not read the DOM or decide which action to run.

Next: [MPA and task continuity](/vanilla/mpa-and-task-continuity).

# MPA and task continuity

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/mpa-and-task-continuity

In a single-page application, a route change usually leaves the document in memory. The page runtime, conversation, and registry survive. A multi-page application is different: following a link unloads the document, and the next page starts with an empty runtime.

Task continuity addresses that difference without pretending the old page still exists. The next document restores a bounded description of the task, then declares its own controls and observes its own page.

## Define what survives navigation

The same continuity setting is used on both documents:

```ts
export const agentSetup: AgentSetup = {
  continuity: {
    resume: "auto",
    returnOnDone: true,
  },
  config: { limits: { maxTurns: 100 } },
};
```

The checkpoint contains the original goal, a bounded page description, recent messages and events, a summary, the task status, and the page where it started. It does not contain DOM nodes, element references, pending approvals, screenshots, cookies, or raw sensitive values.

The next page rebuilds the system prompt from its own declarations. The model sees the old conversation and the new page snapshot together. It cannot invoke an action merely because the action existed on the previous page.

## Create one runtime per document

Each document creates its own runtime and one dock. The list page declares its rows and links; the detail page declares its form and actions:

```ts
const pling = createPling({ agent: agentSetup });
pling.registry.setPage({ path: "/demo/index.html", title: "Customer follow-up" });

pling.dock({ title: "Customer assistant" });
```

```ts
const pling = createPling({ agent: agentSetup });
pling.registry.setPage({ path: "/demo/detail.html", title: `${customer.name} · Customer detail` });

pling.dock({ title: "Customer assistant" });
```

Continuity works when the documents share the same origin, the same tab, and the same storage key. The default key is `pling:continuity`; use a distinct key when one tab intentionally hosts independent tasks.

One tab should have one surface writing a continuity checkpoint. Two docks that enable continuity in the same tab will overwrite each other.

## Choose how the next page resumes

`resume` has three useful settings:

| Value | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `"ask"` (default) | Show a “continue previous task” entry; send nothing until the person chooses it |
| `"auto"` | Send one controlled continuation message after the new page is ready |
| `"off"` | Restore context but do not offer or send a continuation |

`"auto"` does not bypass the agent loop. The model still observes the new page, chooses a declared action, and passes the normal approval and availability checks. It only removes the second request for the original goal.

`returnOnDone` is optional. When it is enabled, the dock returns to the page where the task started after the loop produces a final answer. The destination must be same-origin, and the return action is consumed once.

## Treat an interrupted step as unknown

If the document unloads while an action is running, the conversation may contain an assistant tool call without a matching tool result. Sending that history directly to a model is invalid, and guessing a successful result would be worse.

The restored conversation therefore inserts a synthetic result saying that the document navigated during the step and the outcome is unknown. The model must observe the new page before continuing. This is deliberately conservative: a retry after a real side effect is more dangerous than asking the page what happened.

## Keep business data separate

Continuity carries the task, not the application's data. The example stores its customer data under a business-owned key. The Pling checkpoint is a separate entry.

Do not store authorization tokens, provider keys, or unredacted personal data in either place. A restored conversation is still untrusted input, and a cached page snapshot is not a statement of present business state.

## Run the example

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-11
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5276/demo/index.html?lang=en`, or use `--locale zh` for the Chinese copy. Ask the assistant to set Globex's follow-up note to “Friday dinner”. The list page navigates as a normal document, the detail page continues the task, and the finished task returns to the list once.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-11
```

The checks cover real link navigation, the detail page's ordinary actions, restoration of the goal and conversation, an interrupted tool call, one-time automatic continuation, and isolation in a new tab.

## Common failures

**Expecting the DOM to be restored.** Continuity restores task context, not elements. Each document must declare its own capabilities.

**Using continuity for a client-side route change.** A route that does not unload the document should expose its page identity instead; adding continuity duplicates state for no benefit.

**Assuming a restored task is authorized.** The next page still needs an authenticated session, a valid scope, and confirmation for dangerous actions.

**Returning to an arbitrary URL.** Keep the return target same-origin and validate it as part of the task's starting context.

**Storing raw values in the checkpoint.** Checkpoints are long-lived browser storage. Declare sensitive fields as tokens and keep raw values out of conversation and business storage.

Next: [Test and debug vanilla capabilities](/vanilla/test-and-debug-vanilla-capabilities).

# Test and debug vanilla capabilities

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/test-and-debug-vanilla-capabilities

An agent can fail in several places that look similar in the chat window. A control may never have been declared. The declaration may exist but be unavailable. The model may choose the wrong action. The action may run and still leave the page unchanged. A useful test suite separates those cases instead of asserting only that the final paragraph sounds plausible.

The example is a small work queue. Its page already has ordinary DOM controls. Pling adds a region, one input action, one submit action, and one action per visible row. The same page is used for all checks below.

## Test three boundaries

Start with the declaration boundary. This test reads the registry and asserts what the page actually published.

```ts
const snapshot = pling.registry.snapshot();

expect(snapshot.scopes.find((scope) => scope.id === "todo")).toMatchObject({ role: "main" });
expect(snapshot.records.map((record) => record.id)).toEqual(["t1", "t2", "t3"]);
expect(snapshot.actions.map((action) => action.id)).toContain("composer_text");
expect(snapshot.actions.map((action) => action.id)).not.toContain("composer_submit");
```

The last assertion is not incidental. The submit button is unavailable while the text field is empty, so its action is absent from that snapshot. If it appeared anyway, the page and the model would be working from different states.

The second boundary is execution. Use the same registry and a deterministic policy, then check the business object and the DOM:

```ts
const executor = createExecutor({
  registry: pling.registry,
  policy: createPolicy(async () => true),
});

await executor.execute("composer_text", JSON.stringify({ text: "Write the regression note" }));
await executor.execute("composer_submit", "{}");

expect(tasks[0]).toMatchObject({ text: "Write the regression note", done: false });
expect(document.querySelectorAll(".task")).toHaveLength(4);
```

This check does not start a model loop and does not need a gateway. It answers a narrower question: when the page accepts this action, does it change the object the UI is rendering?

The third boundary is the agent loop. Replace the remote model with a replay script:

```ts
const llm = createReplayLlm([
  { calls: [{ tool: "composer_text", args: { text: "Verify the trace" } }] },
  { calls: [{ tool: "composer_submit" }] },
  { content: "The task was added." },
]);

await dock.runtime.session.send("Add a task named Verify the trace");
```

The replay emits the same tool protocol as a model. It exercises availability calculation, execution, result messages, and the next request. It does not pretend that language understanding has been tested.

## Inspect the exact request

Set `trace` when the development build needs to explain what happened:

```ts
createPling({
  agent: {
    trace: { maxCalls: 8 },
    config: { limits: { maxTurns: 100 } },
  },
});
```

The trace is opt-in and bounded. Each retained call contains the messages, function tools, page snapshot, response, status, duration, and context estimate that were present for that request.

```ts
const trace = dock.runtime.trace;

expect(trace?.calls).toHaveLength(3);
expect(trace?.calls[0]?.messages.map((message) => message.role)).toEqual(["system", "user"]);
expect(trace?.calls[0]?.tools.map((tool) => tool.function.name)).toContain("composer_text");
expect(trace?.calls[1]?.tools.map((tool) => tool.function.name)).toContain("composer_submit");
```

Use the trace to answer four questions in order:

1. Did the first request contain the instruction?
2. Did it contain the intended action and the current record?
3. Did the next request contain the tool call and its result?
4. Did the final page match what the response claimed?

The trace is a development aid. It contains outgoing model context, so production should  leave it off unless access is restricted.

## Test failures as first-class outcomes

A model gateway can be offline. A declaration can be unavailable. A business handler can reject a value. These are different outcomes and should produce different assertions.

The example records a failed request with its structured code instead of reducing it to an empty answer:

```ts
await dock.runtime.session.send("Hello");

expect(dock.runtime.trace?.calls[0]).toMatchObject({
  turn: 1,
  status: "error",
  error: { code: "LLM_FAILED", message: "gateway offline" },
});
```

Keep a small real-model suite if the product depends on intent selection. Run it separately from the deterministic suite, record the model and prompt version, and do not make every pull request depend on a network service.

## Run the example

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-12
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5277/?lang=en`. The page uses the same queue for human controls and replay-driven tests.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-12
```

The check type-checks the example, runs the declaration, execution, replay, trace, and failure tests, and produces a production build.

## Common mistakes

**Asserting exact model prose.** Wording changes without a behavioural regression. Assert page state, returned codes, tools used, and the messages required for the workflow.

**Testing the model first.** If the declaration or executor is wrong, a model test only adds noise. Verify the deterministic layers before involving a provider.

**Leaving tracing on everywhere.** The trace stores system prompts and page snapshots in memory. Treat it as a debugging surface with an explicit access boundary.

**Using sleeps instead of observable conditions.** Wait for a record, a result, or a status transition. Arbitrary delays make tests slow and still race.

Next: [Add Pling to an existing jQuery app](/vanilla/add-pling-to-an-existing-jquery-app).

# Add Pling to an existing jQuery app

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/add-pling-to-an-existing-jquery-app

Many production pages still use jQuery for rendering and event handling. Replacing that code is usually a larger change than the capability work itself. Pling does not require the page to become a component application first. The vanilla adapter attaches to the DOM elements and business objects the page already owns.

This example keeps the queue state in a normal array, renders rows with jQuery, and handles user events with jQuery. Pling declares the region, the input, the submit button, and the row controls. There is no second store and no parallel rendering path.

## Attach at the element boundary

Register the region before its children. The declaration writes the scope marker to the element, so child actions can resolve the same region without repeating its name.

```ts
pling.scope(todo[0], {
  id: "todo",
  label: copy.regionLabel,
  description: copy.regionDescription,
  role: "main",
});
```

The input already exists and jQuery already listens for its `input` event. The capability declaration only says how the agent may fill it:

```ts
pling.tool(input[0], {
  id: "composer_text",
  desc: copy.composerTextDesc,
  action: "fill",
  params: [{ name: "text", label: copy.textParamLabel }],
});
```

The submit action does not call `addTask` directly because the existing form submission already owns that path. Pling performs the same visible operation and lets the existing handler mutate the page.

```ts
pling.tool(submit[0], {
  id: "composer_submit",
  desc: copy.composerSubmitDesc,
  available: () => input.val()?.toString().trim() ? true : copy.submitReason,
});
```

Keeping the existing handler is important. If the agent path called a second `addTask` implementation, human and agent actions could drift in validation, rendering, or side effects.

## Bind records to the live object

Each row is created as a jQuery element, but the record points at the same task object that the click handler mutates:

```ts
const task = { id: "t4", text: "Check the renewal", done: false };
const row = $("<li>").addClass("task");

pling.record(row[0], {
  data: task,
  label: copy.recordLabel(task.text),
});
```

Do not copy task fields into a separate agent-only object. A copied record becomes stale as soon as the page toggles a checkbox. The record should read the same state that the operator sees.

Row actions use stable ids derived from the business id:

```ts
pling.tool(check[0], {
  id: `toggle@${task.id}`,
  desc: copy.toggleDesc(task.text, task.done),
});
```

The index in the jQuery collection is not an identity. Sorting, filtering, or inserting a row changes it. `t4` remains valid until that task is actually removed.

## Remove declarations with the DOM

When a row is removed, unbind its Pling declarations and its jQuery handlers together. The example keeps both in the same lifecycle so the next render cannot leave a registered action pointing at a detached element.

The same rule applies when a page fragment is replaced through `.html()` or a template refresh. Removing DOM nodes does not automatically remove their registry entries. Keep the cleanup function returned by every `pling.tool`, `pling.record`, and `pling.scope` call.

## Migrate in one narrow slice

A safe adoption sequence for an existing page is:

1. Choose one business task with a stable object and a visible result.
2. Keep the current jQuery handlers and state.
3. Declare the region and only the controls needed for that task.
4. Add records for the rows or values the agent must distinguish.
5. Put a deterministic test around the existing handler.
6. Expand only after the first slice is reliable.

This order avoids a rewrite whose only purpose is to satisfy the Agent integration. It also makes rollback simple: remove the declarations and the page remains the same jQuery application.

## Run the example

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-13
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5278/?lang=en`, or pass `--locale zh` and open `http://127.0.0.1:5278/?lang=zh`.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-13
```

The check installs the release-equivalent packages, compiles the jQuery and TypeScript surface, runs the end-to-end tests, and builds the page.

## Common mistakes

**Creating a second task array for Pling.** The agent would modify a copy while the table renders the original. Bind records to the active object.

**Relying on jQuery selectors as action ids.** A selector can match a different row after a sort. Use a stable business id and keep the selector only as an implementation detail.

**Forgetting `.off()` and the Pling cleanup.** Replacing a row without removing either lifecycle leaves duplicate handlers or stale capabilities.

**Reimplementing submit inside `run`.** Reuse the existing business function or DOM event path so both users and agents receive the same validation and side effects.

Next: [Expose selected capabilities to external agents](/vanilla/expose-selected-capabilities-to-external-agents).

# Expose selected capabilities to external agents

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vanilla/expose-selected-capabilities-to-external-agents

The assistant inside a page and an external agent should not need two implementations of the same business operation. Both can use the page's existing action executor. What differs is discovery and transport: an external client needs a bounded description of what this site exposes and a protocol boundary through which it can invoke those operations.

Agent Surface is that boundary. It is not a second action system, and it is not a browser-automation escape hatch. It publishes a selected set of already declared actions and sends each invocation through the same availability, confirmation, expectation, and result path used by the page assistant.

## Start from the page, not the protocol

The example page has three useful business operations:

- `todo.overview` reads the queue counts.
- `todo.add` adds one task with bounded text input.
- `todo.clear_completed` removes completed tasks and requires confirmation.

The page also has row-level completion controls, but they are not part of the external allowlist. The external surface is deliberately smaller than the page. This is a product and security decision, not an omission.

```ts
export const EXTERNAL_SCOPE = [
  "todo.overview",
  "todo.add",
  "todo.clear_completed",
] as const;
```

Capability ids should describe business intent and stay stable across rendering changes. A selector, row position, or localized button label is not a stable capability name.

## Reuse the executor

The Surface kernel receives a projection of the registry and an execution function:

```ts
const executor = createExecutor({
  registry,
  policy: createPolicy(confirm),
  settle: defaultSettle,
});

const surface = createSurface({
  registry,
  execute: (id, args) => executor.execute(id, args),
  app: "tutorial-support-queue",
  expose: EXTERNAL_SCOPE,
  session,
  recordLimit: 2,
});
```

This arrangement keeps execution in one place. The external call does not click a DOM element, call a private handler, or bypass the confirmation policy. If the page action is unavailable, the same availability reason applies. If its result fails, the executor returns the same error.

## Describe must be narrow

An external client first calls `describe`. The response contains the protocol version, application name, allowed capabilities, and a bounded context window.

```ts
const response = await surface.handle({
  protocol: SURFACE_PROTOCOL,
  id: "req_01",
  method: "describe",
  input: { limit: 2 },
});
```

The example publishes only the three allowlisted capability ids and returns two records even though the page contains three. `recordLimit` and the requested limit keep context cost explicit. A larger list needs pagination or a search action; the protocol should not serialize an unbounded table merely because it exists in the page.

The description is generated from the live registry. It does not serialize internal handlers, DOM selectors, session cookies, or unrelated business state.

## Invoke returns two kinds of failure

An invocation can fail before reaching the action because the capability is not exposed:

```ts
{
  ok: false,
  error: { code: "CAPABILITY_NOT_EXPOSED", message: "..." }
}
```

Or the protocol exchange can succeed while the business action fails:

```ts
{
  ok: true,
  result: {
    error: { code: "PERMISSION_DENIED", message: "..." }
  }
}
```

Clients must handle both. Checking only `response.ok` would report a denied write as a successful protocol call.

The example tests an unexposed row action directly. It is rejected before the executor, and the task remains unchanged. That fail-closed boundary is what makes the allowlist meaningful.

## Keep confirmation in the page

`todo.clear_completed` is destructive and declared with `confirm: "always"`. When an external client invokes it, the executor opens the page-side confirmation channel and waits.

The external client cannot approve its own request. A person sees the pending action in the page and decides. If denied, the protocol exchange completes with `PERMISSION_DENIED`; if approved, the existing business handler runs once.

```ts
const pending = surface.handle({
  protocol: SURFACE_PROTOCOL,
  id: "req_02",
  method: "invoke",
  capability: "todo.clear_completed",
});

// The page renders the approval decision.
const result = await pending;
```

This is also why the approval UI belongs to the application, not to the external agent's console. The client may display progress, but the trusted decision surface remains with the signed-in page.

## Identity and transport sit outside the kernel

The `session` passed to Surface is already verified. It contains the agent id, session id, user id, expiry, and the session's capability scope. It does not contain a password, cookie, OAuth token, or provider key.

A deployment still needs a transport adapter to:

- authenticate the user and the external agent;
- validate origin and request size;
- create, expire, and revoke the delegated session;
- apply rate limits and replay protection;
- attach request ids and deliver audit records.

HTTP, an MCP facade, and a postMessage bridge can all carry the same `describe` and `invoke` envelope. They should not reimplement capability filtering or confirmation.

## Run the example

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev j-14
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5279/?lang=en`, or use `--locale zh` and open `http://127.0.0.1:5279/?lang=zh`. The right-hand console calls only `surface.handle()`. It can describe the capability set, add a task, and request removal of completed tasks.

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check j-14
```

The check covers the capability allowlist, bounded records, a successful write, an unexposed action, denial, approval, and removal of the row's remaining declarations.

## Common mistakes

**Publishing every registered action.** The external surface should be a smaller, intentional product interface. A page may offer dozens of controls while exposing three operations.

**Treating a synchronous function as authenticated.** A session object is data. The transport must verify the caller before Surface receives it.

**Adding a generic click or script method.** That turns the surface back into browser automation and makes the allowlist ineffective.

**Showing approval in the external client.** A client that can approve its own destructive request has not added a meaningful human check.

**Returning the entire page snapshot.** Context should be bounded, deterministic, and limited to what the capability needs.

Return to the [Vanilla and jQuery overview](/vanilla/) or read the [Agent Surface introduction](/surface/).

# Vue 2 support statement

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vue2/

`@plingjs/vue2` connects an existing Vue 2.7 application to Pling. It is an adapter, not a fork of the Vue 3 integration. The application keeps its components, state, event handlers, and rendering model. Pling adds a capability registry, a set of directives, and a DOM-based assistant entry.

`@plingjs/vue2` supports Vue 2.7. Vue 2.6 and earlier do not provide the Composition API this adapter uses, so they cannot use it; those projects can still declare page capabilities manually through `@plingjs/vanilla`. The two integration paths have different boundaries. Vue 3 uses `@plingjs/vue`, which has different installation code and a separate learning path.

## Choosing a version

| Project version | Integration | What it provides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vue 2.7 | `@plingjs/vue2` | `v-tool`, `v-scope`, `v-record`, state helpers, and lifecycle cleanup |
| Vue 2.6 and earlier | `@plingjs/vanilla` | Manual `pling.tool()`, `pling.scope()`, `pling.record()`, `pling.state()`, and `pling.dock()` calls after the component mounts |

If the project can be upgraded, move to Vue 2.7 first and use `@plingjs/vue2`. When that is not possible, the Vanilla path can still connect an existing page to Pling. The cost is that declarations and cleanup remain explicit application code.

## What the adapter provides

| Need | Vue 2.7 form |
| --- | --- |
| Create and install the runtime | `createPling()`, then `Vue.use(pling.plugin)` |
| Describe a page region | `v-scope` |
| Describe a control | `v-tool` |
| Describe a row or other business record | `v-record` |
| Read a selected state view | `useAgentState()` or `useAgentStoreState()` |
| Mount the assistant | `pling.dock()` |

`pling.dock()` is the shared DOM assistant. The Vue 2 adapter does not ship a second chat renderer that behaves differently from the Vue 3 and vanilla adapters.

## What it does not provide

- It does not give a Vue 2.6 application `v-tool`, `v-scope`, `v-record`, or `useAgentState()`. Those projects should use `@plingjs/vanilla` instead.
- It does not take over routing, state management, form submission, or server persistence.
- It does not replace accessibility attributes or server-side authorization.
- It does not make a Vue 2 application equivalent to a Vue 3 application. The supported APIs and the recommended migration path remain distinct.

The adapter is suitable when an application is already on Vue 2.7 and needs a controlled way to expose selected controls to an agent. A new application should generally start on Vue 3. For an older application, begin with the smallest useful declaration and expand only where the business operation is understood.

The Vanilla path for Vue 2.6 and earlier has no adapter managing declarations. Unbind each declaration when the component is destroyed, and register records and row actions again after the list renders. See [Install and first mount](/vue2/install-and-first-mount) for the concrete pattern.

## Integration boundary

Integration code belongs in the page entry and in the templates or render functions that already own the business controls. The agent executes a declared control through the same browser event path a person uses:

1. The adapter registers the element or region.
2. The executor resolves the declared action.
3. The browser dispatches the click, input, or form event.
4. The existing Vue handler updates the application.
5. The next registry snapshot reflects the resulting page state.

This order matters. A declaration is not a second business implementation, and a successful click is not by itself proof that a remote server accepted the change.

Continue with [Install and first mount](/vue2/install-and-first-mount).

---

# Install and first mount

Canonical: https://plingjs.dev/vue2/install-and-first-mount

This chapter connects a Vue 2.7 page to one Pling runtime and one assistant entry. The page still has no declared actions, so the assistant can explain what it sees but cannot operate a business control yet.

## Install the adapter

Install `@plingjs/vue2` with the package manager already used by the application:

| Package manager | Command |
| --- | --- |
| pnpm | `pnpm add @plingjs/vue2` |
| npm | `npm install @plingjs/vue2` |
| Yarn | `yarn add @plingjs/vue2` |

The adapter requires Vue 2.7. It uses the shared DOM execution layer; it does not replace Vue's renderer or event system.

## Create and install the runtime

Create the runtime once in the page entry and install its Vue plugin before mounting the application:

```ts
import Vue from "vue";
import { createPling } from "@plingjs/vue2";

const pling = createPling({
  ui: { locale: "en-US" },
  agent: {
    config: {
      systemPrompt: "You are the assistant for this page. Keep answers short.",
      limits: { maxTurns: 100 },
    },
  },
});

Vue.use(pling.plugin);
```

`Vue.use(pling.plugin)` registers `v-tool`, `v-scope`, and `v-record`. It does not register actions by itself; a control becomes visible to the agent only after the page declares it.

In a real application, the model endpoint and credentials should normally be supplied by a server-side gateway. The browser must not receive a production provider secret merely to make the assistant appear.

## Mount the assistant entry

The shared DOM dock is mounted after the Vue instance exists:

```ts
new Vue({
  data() {
    return { dock: null };
  },
  mounted() {
    this.dock = pling.dock({
      title: "Page assistant",
      quick: ["What can you do on this page?"],
    });
  },
  beforeDestroy() {
    this.dock?.destroy();
  },
  render(h) {
    return h("main", "A normal Vue 2.7 page");
  },
}).$mount("#app");
```

Destroy the dock and the Pling runtime when the page or micro-frontend is torn down. Leaving a runtime attached after its application has gone away produces stale registrations and duplicate assistant entries.

## Check the first mount

Run the example:

```bash
pnpm tutorial:dev v2-02
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5242/`. For the Chinese interface, run `pnpm tutorial:dev v2-02 --locale zh` and open `http://127.0.0.1:5242/?lang=zh`.

The deterministic check is:

```bash
pnpm tutorial:check v2-02
```

It verifies the Vue 2.7 mount, plugin installation, assistant entry, and absence of page actions.

## Common failures

**Installing the plugin after mounting the application.** The directives must be registered before the templates that use them are compiled. Put `Vue.use(pling.plugin)` in the entry before `new Vue(...).$mount(...)`.

**Creating more than one runtime.** A page should have one Pling instance and one assistant entry. Create it in the application entry, not inside a row or a repeated component.

**Assuming the assistant has page authority.** The entry only provides a conversation surface. A control that never receives `v-tool` is not in the registry, even if it is visible to a person.

## Vue 2.6 and earlier: use the Vanilla adapter

Vue 2.6 and earlier cannot use `@plingjs/vue2`, because that adapter depends on the Vue 2.7 Composition API. The project does not have to remain outside Pling: `@plingjs/vanilla` has no Vue dependency, so it can bind the DOM elements a component has already rendered.

This path has no directives and no adapter-managed lifecycle. The application calls `pling.tool()`, `pling.scope()`, `pling.record()`, and `pling.state()` after the component mounts. Each call returns an unbind function, and row records and row actions must be registered again when the list renders.

### Install

Keep the existing Vue 2.6 installation and add only the Vanilla adapter:

| Package manager | Command |
| --- | --- |
| pnpm | `pnpm add @plingjs/vanilla` |
| npm | `npm install @plingjs/vanilla` |
| Yarn | `yarn add @plingjs/vanilla` |

Do not install `@plingjs/vue2`, and do not call `Vue.use()`. The existing bundler must be able to consume the package's ESM output; this is independent of the Vue version. The Pling runtime targets browsers with ES2022 modules, and using Vue 2.6 does not change that requirement. If the application still supports older browsers, evaluate transpilation and polyfills first.

### Create the runtime in the entry

Create one instance at the application entry and pass it to the root component with `provide`:

```ts
import Vue from "vue";
import { createPling } from "@plingjs/vanilla";
import App from "./App.vue";

const pling = createPling({
  ui: { locale: "en-US" },
  agent: {
    config: {
      baseUrl: "/llm/v1",
      model: "your-model",
      limits: { maxTurns: 100 },
    },
  },
});

new Vue({
  provide: { pling },
  render: (h) => h(App),
}).$mount("#app");
```

The model endpoint should still point at a server-side gateway. The browser receives the gateway URL, not a production provider secret.

### Declare capabilities in an Options API component

The component below keeps ordinary Vue 2.6 data and event handlers. Pling reads those elements, invokes the same handlers, and exposes read-only counts through `pling.state()`:

```vue
<template>
  <main ref="app">
    <form @submit.prevent="addTodo">
      <label for="new-todo">New task</label>
      <input id="new-todo" ref="composer" v-model="draft" />
      <button ref="addButton" type="submit">Add</button>
    </form>

    <ul ref="list">
      <li v-for="todo in todos" :key="todo.id" :data-todo-id="todo.id">
        <input
          data-action="toggle"
          type="checkbox"
          :checked="todo.done"
          @change="toggleTodo(todo.id)"
        />
        <span>{{ todo.text }}</span>
        <button data-action="delete" type="button" @click="removeTodo(todo.id)">
          Delete
        </button>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </main>
</template>

<script>
export default {
  inject: ["pling"],

  data() {
    return {
      draft: "",
      seq: 3,
      todos: [
        { id: "t1", text: "Prepare the weekly meeting notes", done: false },
        { id: "t2", text: "Reply to the customer email", done: true },
      ],
    };
  },

  created() {
    this.rowUnbinds = [];
  },

  mounted() {
    this.pling.scope(this.$refs.app, {
      id: "todo_app",
      label: "Task application",
      role: "main",
    });

    this.pling.tool(this.$refs.composer, {
      id: "todo_text",
      desc: "Fill in the text for a new task",
      action: "fill",
      params: [{ name: "text", label: "Task text" }],
    });

    this.pling.tool(this.$refs.addButton, {
      id: "add_todo",
      desc: "Add the composer text as a task",
      kind: "write",
      available: () => (this.draft.trim() ? true : "The composer is empty"),
    });

    this.pling.state(
      "todo_view",
      () => ({
        total: this.todos.length,
        remaining: this.todos.filter((todo) => !todo.done).length,
      }),
      { description: "Task total and remaining count" },
    );

    this.pling.dock({
      title: "Task assistant",
      quick: ["Add a task called “Write the weekly report”", "Complete the first task"],
    });

    this.syncRows();
  },

  beforeDestroy() {
    this.releaseRows();
    this.pling.destroy();
  },

  methods: {
    async syncRows() {
      await this.$nextTick();
      this.releaseRows();

      for (const todo of this.todos) {
        const row = Array.from(this.$refs.list.children).find(
          (element) => element.dataset.todoId === todo.id,
        );
        if (!row) continue;

        this.rowUnbinds.push(
          this.pling.record(row, { data: todo, label: `Task: ${todo.text}` }),
          this.pling.tool(row.querySelector('[data-action="toggle"]'), {
            id: `toggle_todo:${todo.id}`,
            desc: `Toggle task completion: ${todo.text}`,
            kind: "write",
          }),
          this.pling.tool(row.querySelector('[data-action="delete"]'), {
            id: `delete_todo:${todo.id}`,
            desc: `Delete task: ${todo.text}`,
            kind: "danger",
          }),
        );
      }
    },

    releaseRows() {
      for (const unbind of this.rowUnbinds) unbind();
      this.rowUnbinds = [];
    },

    addTodo() {
      const text = this.draft.trim();
      if (!text) return;

      this.todos.push({ id: `t${this.seq++}`, text, done: false });
      this.draft = "";
      this.syncRows();
    },

    toggleTodo(id) {
      const todo = this.todos.find((item) => item.id === id);
      if (todo) todo.done = !todo.done;
      this.syncRows();
    },

    removeTodo(id) {
      this.todos = this.todos.filter((todo) => todo.id !== id);
      this.syncRows();
    },
  },
};
</script>
```

`v-model`, `@submit`, and `@click` remain Vue's responsibility. `pling.tool()` only connects the model-visible action to those elements. The composer's `fill` action writes the value and dispatches `input`; the submit button then follows the original form path.

`syncRows()` runs again after every list change because adding or removing a task replaces or removes DOM nodes. Unbind the old row declarations first, then register the current nodes; otherwise a declaration can keep pointing at an element that has left the document. Changing only a field on the same row, such as its completion state, does not replace the node Vue keeps, and each snapshot reads the latest value from the same object.

This manual path does not provide `v-tool`, `v-scope`, `v-record`, `useAgentState()`, or automatic lifecycle cleanup. It uses the same `core` / `dom` execution layer as the Vue 2.7 adapter, but the compatibility promise covers only the Vanilla APIs shown here.

Next: [Quick start: a complete Todo agent](/vue2/quick-start).
